In the realm of offline reinforcement learning, we delve into the challenge of learning a robust optimal policy even when the training dataset has been compromised by an adversary altering some of its contents. Focusing on a Markov decision process consisting of d-dimensional tuples and T time steps, we demonstrate that if only a small fraction $\epsilon$ of the dataset's tuples have been modified, the resulting damage is proportional to $\epsilon$. Consequently, we develop an algorithm capable of identifying a near-optimal policy within the compromised dataset, with the policy being no more than $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$ away from the one it would have chosen had the dataset remained unaltered. Furthermore, we establish an irreducible relationship between this outcome and the optimal possible performance in robust reinforcement learning.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximation and finite-time smoothness result involving dynamic boundaries in this context.

A consensus has not been reached on how to define or detect out-of-distribution examples, particularly since different methods show varying performance depending on the type of shift, as demonstrated in recent studies. To address this issue, we investigate a range of anomaly detection techniques, analyzing their resilience to various types of shifts, including domain, semantic, and syntactic anomalies. Our research reveals that, contrary to previous findings, a single method, ensemble of energy-based models, achieves superior results across all anomaly types, outperforming other methods, including human evaluation, and surprisingly, even the human brain.

We have developed a new theoretical model for creating artificial molecular machines that operate using electrical currents. In contrast to previously known designs which used light or chemical energy, our model takes advantage of the fact that electrical currents can modify the properties of conductive molecules through electrochemical effects. As a result, our proposed molecular machines can operate indefinitely without needing to constantly replenish their fuel supply. Initially, we created simple models for electrical motors that operate using electrical currents in both classical and quantum regimes. Then, we explored the possibility of creating more sophisticated artificial molecules with electrical memory by exploiting the permanent changes in conductive molecules caused by electrical currents. These special molecules can "remember" past current flows by changing their electrical conductance based on the direction and magnitude of previous currents. Our results indicate that such electrical molecules have the potential to be used as the basis for novel memory storage materials and innovative molecular computing systems.

Building on a 2017 study by Kuperberg and Mohri on transducer semantics, we investigate various interpretations and operational frameworks, comparing them to the standard transducer model used in automata theory. Our analysis reveals that although some interpretations appear similar to the standard model, others give rise to distinct and significant notions of language acceptance and recognisation. We demonstrate that certain operations, including changing transducer directions and forming the inverse of a transducer, remain consistent across different interpretations, whereas others, like composing transducers, vary significantly. Our findings show that while some decision problems are solvable for all transducer semantics, others are only decidable under specific conditions, such as limited transducer branching.

In this study, we investigate the fundamental concept of the $f$-Convolution, a generalized approach to standard convolution, where the product of values is substituted by an arbitrary function $f$. By employing a straightforward method, the $f$-Convolution of two functions, $f$ and $g$, each defined on $n$ elements, can be computed in $O(n^2)$ operations. The specific case of the standard convolution, known as the convolution product, can be computed in $O(n \log n)$ or $O(n \log^2 n)$ steps using well-known algorithms. The broader objective is to identify the optimal time frame for computing the $f$-Convolution, particularly when the function $f$ is not necessarily commutative. The problem becomes even more complex when we consider that the function $f$ is defined by a lookup table of size $O(n)$. In this context, we explore a broader class of functions, denoted as $\mathcal{F}$, that are defined on sets of size $n$ and map to sets of size $n$. The $\mathcal{F}$-Convolution, a convolution generalized to a function $f$ belonging to the $\mathcal{F}$ class, is another instance of the $f$-Convolution problem.

The 1998 discovery of GJ 229B marked a significant breakthrough in astronomy, 
as it provided crucial insights into the physical and chemical composition of 
late T dwarfs. Since then, multiple spectroscopic studies have been conducted 
to refine our understanding of GJ 229B, each employing diverse analysis methods. 
A recent study utilizes modern spectroscopic retrieval techniques to determine 
GJ 229B's physical properties. By combining near-infrared and visible spectra 
with a comprehensive model, researchers found that GJ 229B has a mass of 
0.049$^{+0.013}_{-0.009}$ M$_{\rm J}$, an effective temperature of 
770$^{+30}_{-40}$ K, and an age of 4.8$^{+1.3}_{-1.0}$ Gyr. Additionally, 
these findings indicate that GJ 229B possesses a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere 
with a methane mixing ratio of 0.23, consistent with expectations. 
Notably, this study also highlights the importance of incorporating UV and X-ray 
spectra into atmospheric retrievals to gain a more comprehensive understanding 
of exoplanet atmospheres.

Our research focuses on the lattice QCD simulation of two-light-quark states coupled with heavy-quark currents, specifically in the pseudoscalar sector with $J^{PC}=0^{++}$, in the region around or below 2 GeV. We conducted calculations using $N_f=2$ Wilson fermions on $N_c=3$ lattices with four different heavy-quark currents. These simulations were performed on $8^3\times 8$ lattices with $N_f=2$ Wilson fermions. We analyzed the spectral density and found that the spectral density at very low energies is dominated by noise. We also investigated the correlation functions and found that they are consistent with the expectations for pseudoscalar states with $0^{++}$ quantum numbers. However, we found that the energy of the pseudoscalar states is higher than the sum of the energies of the vector and pseudoscalar heavy-quark states. This suggests that the correlation functions are likely influenced by states other than the ground state. Based on these findings, we conclude that the existence of a $0^{++}$ exotic state below 2 GeV is unlikely.

A crucial objective of the LHCb experiment at CERN is to investigate the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ in the $B_{s}^{0}$ system by studying hadronic decays like $B_{s}^{0}\to J/\psi K^{0}$ and $B_{s}^{0}\to DD^{(*)\pm K^{\mp}$. The experiment will also analyze recent findings and future capabilities in accessing $\phi_{s}$ through hadronic decays and discuss prospects for measuring $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ using hadronic $B_{s}^{0}$ decays such as $B_{s}^{0}\to K^{+}K^{-}$ and $B_{s}^{0}\to H^{0}H^{+}$ in the full Run 2+Run 3 dataset and LHCb Upgrade.

Airborne transmission of pathogens in confined areas is a pressing concern, and understanding the behavior of suspended particles is crucial. A mathematical model is developed to simulate the movement of aerosols within a rectangular chamber, taking into consideration the complex dynamics of virus-carrying particles. By incorporating coagulation and breakup processes, the model accounts for the interaction of aerosols with room occupants and ventilation systems. Analytical solutions are derived for scenarios involving the introduction of aerosols through uniform mixing or localized sources, and these solutions are validated through numerical computations. Ultimately, the model provides a framework for estimating the concentration of infectious particles in indoor environments, and this knowledge is essential for developing effective public health measures.

We conducted an analysis of $\beta$-decay related metrics, including $\ft$, $\beta$-decay shape correction, and ft values, for specific isotopes such as $^{52}$Mn, $^{54}$Co, $^{56}$Co, and $^{57}$Co. Additionally, ft values for several other even-odd isotopes were estimated for the first time, such as $^{53}$Mn, $^{55}$Co, and others. Our analysis involved comparing the calculated metrics with available experimental data, as well as the results from the Monte Carlo Shell Model and the interacting shell-model. Our findings indicate that the ISM offers a more accurate representation, particularly for the $\beta$-decay shape correction, while Monte Carlo Shell Model tends to underestimate this parameter. Our analysis also included an examination of the energy differences between the initial and final states in the $\beta$-decay process, as well as the properties of the initial and final states, including their spin and parity. Our analysis indicates that the ISM offers a more accurate representation of the spin and parity properties, as well as the energy differences, while Monte Carlo Shell Model tends to overestimate the spin and parity properties. Our analysis also included an examination of the radial and angular components of the wave functions, as well as the properties of the single-particle states, and found that the ISM offers a more accurate representation of the spin and parity properties, as

Double-sided auctions are a fundamental concept in economics, widely used in markets that quantify goods in discrete units. Although the typical auction model is designed for a single quantity of a good, our work expands on this concept, adapting it to accommodate any quantity and demonstrating its feasibility through a rigorous mathematical proof. As a result, our formulation holds significant value in financial markets, where trade quantities are often substantial and complex, and offers the potential to improve existing mechanisms in these areas.

We use heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying this framework to the lightest bottom mesons as well. By examining the mass spectra of these mesons, their decay modes, and the partial widths associated with their decays into lighter hadrons, we utilize the Spontaneous Chiral Symmetry Breaking model to analyze $B$ mesons, while employing the SU(4) heavy quark symmetry model for $B_s$ mesons. Our calculations, which incorporate linear interpolation to estimate masses for excited $B$ mesons, reveal a striking resemblance between our theoretical predictions and the experimentally observed results for $B$ mesons that have been reported by the BESIII collaboration.

We demonstrate that a regular line's nonexpansive properties are present in all its periodic configurations. Furthermore, the periodic configurations of a given line can be reorganized into an ordered sequence based on their minimum possible configurations. The lengths of this ordered sequence follow a predictable pattern that can be calculated using a specific formula derived from the characteristics of the regular line itself. The concept of the monoid of minimal configurations on a regular line is explored and its algebraic properties are analyzed. The concept of the monoid of periodic configurations is also introduced and its structure is defined based on the properties of the regular line itself.

Modeling complex systems with modern data-driven approaches often poses significant challenges, particularly in cases where data is high-dimensional, comes from multiple sources, or exhibits sparse behavior. To address these issues, we introduce the dynamic sparse subspace model, a data-driven method capable of capturing evolving, high-dimensional, and sparse data patterns. The model's mathematical framework relies on the dynamic spatial subspace model, enhanced with L1-norm regularization to promote sparsity. We evaluate the dynamic sparse subspace model in simulation studies comparing it with established models and also apply it to analyze real-world data from the New York City taxi dataset.

In competitive chess, the choice of opening moves significantly impacts the outcome.
Coaches often advise players to stick to their established opening routines, but
without clear guidance on whether these strategies remain effective against
different opponents. To address this, we introduce a novel concept: the relatedness
network of chess openings, which groups similar opening strategies and identifies
those associated with opposing opponents. Our analysis, based on over 20 million
games from the Chess.com database, reveals that similar opening strategies yield
consistent results, regardless of the opponent chosen, and opponents employing
unexpected opening tactics tend to be at a disadvantage. These findings have the
potential to inform players and coaches in refining their opening strategies. To
facilitate further research, we have developed a publicly accessible network
representation of popular opening strategies, which can be utilized to analyze
relatedness and provide actionable insights.

This research focuses on the characteristics of millisecond pulsars, particularly their masses, ages, spin rates, and magnetic field strengths, which are examined through a study of their birth and evolution. A theoretical model is established to analyze the formation and evolution of binary pulsars, incorporating various processes such as mass transfer, mass loss, and magnetic field changes. The investigation reveals that the mass ratio of the pulsar system is primarily influenced by the initial properties of the stars, and that the pulsar's age and spin rate are largely determined by the mass transfer dynamics, while the system's magnetic field strength is found to be relatively uniform and unaffected by these dynamics. The comparison of the model's predictions with observational data shows a discrepancy in the distribution of magnetic field strengths, and suggests that additional factors, such as the evolution of the pulsar's companion star, may need to be considered.

A method to find conserved quantities for ordinary differential equations of second order, which may be nonlinear, is outlined in this paper. We derive an expression for these constants of motion and demonstrate their applicability with two examples, ultimately obtaining improved existence and analytical bounds for differential equations of second order, leading to new bounds for dissipative mechanical systems, despite not being conservative.

This study introduces a novel technique that enables users to reconstruct three-dimensional models by sketching in mid-air using a simple tool similar to a wand. The technique leverages the capabilities of implicit neural representations and a geometric constraint-based method to produce robust results even when the initial sketch is two-dimensional. To facilitate this, we developed SNEK (Sketch Anything Nerf-Kinect), which incorporates depth information to enhance model reconstruction. Additionally, we incorporated user feedback through hard-margin support vector classification to further improve the reconstruction quality. This technique can be executed in a virtual reality environment using just a single device, such as the Microsoft Kinect for its ease of use.

This paper presents a detailed analysis of the upcoming TRAPPIST-3b planet, which was discovered as part of the same survey that led to the identification of the seven planets in the TRAPPIST-1 system. Although its existence is confirmed, limited data was obtained due to its smaller size and wider orbital distance from its host star. A comprehensive study was conducted to assess the insolation, planetary parameters, and atmospheric potential of TRAPPIST-3b, which is similar to its neighboring planets in terms of insolation and orbital period. As a result, an extensive search for atmospheric signatures was proposed using current and upcoming telescopes, which could provide valuable insights into the planet's atmospheric composition and habitability.

In order to investigate the local and global characteristics of an anisotropic homogeneous spacetime representing a fluid with isotropic stress, we examined its gravitational collapse. We started by assuming the fluid's pressure equals zero, which led to one partial differential equation and another algebraic equation governing the fluid's energy density and two metric variables. We found the two equations governing the fluid's energy density and one metric variable are incompatible, which implies the fluid cannot sustain isotropic stress. We then derived two evolution equations for the fluid's energy density, which are mutually incompatible, which suggests the fluid cannot sustain isotropic pressure. We found that the spacetime represents a vacuum space-time, which is consistent with the Bianchi type II spacetime.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we derived a general expression for the extremality corrections to black hole areas and charges in alternative theories of gravity. Our findings indicate that these corrections to black hole charge are directly related to the violation of various energy conditions. Specifically, in cases where gravity theories reduce to scalar-gravity monomials, we found the extremality corrections to be governed by a single, universal parameter. This discovery confirms existing results for AdS_CML black holes and provides new insights into extremality corrections in gravity with negative AdS radii.

A key challenge in goal-directed motor learning is to uncover underlying regularities in unpredictable task conditions.  To address this issue, a novel behavioral assay has been developed, leveraging reinforcement learning to adapt to changing reward structures.  The system learns to prioritize actions that are robust against uncertainty, similar to how humans and animals respond to increased risk aversion when uncertainty is high.  The concept of robust actions is operationalized through a measure of action's resilience to uncertainty, revealing that the system learns actions with higher resilience in uncertain situations, whereas those with lower resilience are preferred in predictable situations.  The associated software is freely available online.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a foundation for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity in three dimensions. Researchers have derived the associated algebraic curvature invariants and used them to construct the gravity's action. Specifically, they found that incorporating an invariant coloured curvature term results in a simple constraint: the coloured cosmological constant must be equal to zero. This constant's zero value is also reflected in the energy-momentum scalar obtained from a quantum field theory quantum correction to the gravity's action.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying if a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the number of edges, and an exponential-parameter algorithm based on the graph's treewidth. Our approach involves reducing the original problem to finding a valid orientation of the graph's closed form, which we then analyze under various conditions to determine the feasibility of applying existing parameterized methods for directedacyclic graphs.

Image-goal navigation is tackled with the MemoNav system, which utilizes a short-term memory mechanism to navigate towards objectives. Observing the connection between human memory and successful navigation, we designed MemoNav to mimic this relationship. Within the framework of reinforcement learning, we incorporated a memory module that stores and retrieves states, and a attention-based system to connect this module with the main network. Through experimental evaluation on standard datasets, we showed that MemoNav surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, and further analysis revealed the memo structure to be a map-like representation of the environment.

The rapid growth of data traffic driven by various emerging applications has led to an overwhelming demand for licensed spectrum, far exceeding the capacity provided by current cellular networks. Technologies like 5G and D2D have made significant contributions, but they are limited in addressing the overall spectrum scarcity issue. As a result, alternative spectrum sources such as unlicensed microwave and millimeter-wave bands are being explored to bridge the remaining gap. However, these unlicensed frequencies are heavily occupied by microwave links and high-capacity wireless systems, which are prone to signal interference. To tackle this problem, we propose an underlay approach that allows cellular users to safely access these unlicensed frequencies by utilizing advanced signal processing techniques to filter out strong interfering signals. We design a specific microwave signal filter and evaluate its effectiveness through a prototype built on software-defined radio, demonstrating the feasibility of our approach in lab-based experiments.

To model complex interactions between multiple systems, higher-dimensional models are employed.  However, there has been little research on developing similar models for almost periodic systems.  In response to this gap, we develop a high-dimensional model for nearly periodic systems on hypergraphs and prove its existence and uniqueness.  Furthermore, we prove that solutions in such a system will converge to a shared, periodic pattern over time, provided certain conditions are met.  In addition to these theoretical results, we also provide numerical examples to illustrate the accuracy of our findings.

The development of operators in quantum systems is examined within the framework of Lie symmetry, specifically focusing on symmetries like those found in cubic lattices and Weyl-Heisenberg algebras. The study reveals a distinct pattern of operator growth, which is limited to specific irreducible components of the Lie algebra and thus can be quantified in terms of these components. The initial composition of the operator is seen to influence its trajectory of growth in this context. The study also explores the connection between operator growth and the creation of entanglement between a system and its environment, demonstrating that in systems with quadratic Hamiltonians, a specific formula can be used to measure the degree of entanglement created.

To resolve ongoing debates about the structural nature of the Hoyle state, a new approach is taken. By analyzing the direct decay ratio of the Hoyle state into two and three alpha particles, evidence is gathered to support or refute the hypothesis that it is an alpha-condensate. The theoretical framework for this analysis involves calculating the probability of direct decay into two alpha particles using an approximate, extended van der Waals force interaction between the particles. This probability is then compared to an estimated probability of direct decay into three alpha particles, which is derived by considering the probability of one of the final state particles interacting with the remaining resonance state. The results indicate that the calculated ratio is consistent with experimental data, and that this agreement supports the hypothesis that the Hoyle state is composed of predominantly correlated pairs of alpha particles, as evidenced by the dominance of the force between the particles over their self-energy.

Research into crack growth in 2D brittle materials has shown that for fast crack propagation, an oscillatory instability arises, observed in experiments and simulations, but still poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a theoretical analysis of the oscillatory crack problem using an extended Griffith model that accounts for dynamic effects, while assuming a simple atomic bond model, and found that the oscillatory instability arises from a resonance between the crack frequency and a breathing mode of the atomic lattice, influenced by asymmetry in the atomic bond potential. This approach provides a simplified understanding of the oscillatory crack problem and may serve as a foundation for further research.

In 1961, Brown introduced the concept of feedback capacity for stochastic channels. It has since been established that this capacity can be effectively calculated in certain cases, such as when the channel has a finite state or exhibits the strong Markov property. Although the concept is universally applicable to all memoryless channels with finite states, this property is not exclusive to those specific cases. This is particularly evident when the channel experiences cyclic behavior. To address this limitation, an extension of the existing finite state channel model has been developed, which is more general in nature. This modified model has enabled the derivation of new, universally applicable formulas for feedback capacity. These formulas have subsequently been applied to two distinct types of stochastic processes: stable Lévy motion and fractional Brownian motion, which are characterized by specific parameters denoted as α and H, respectively.

Rashba spin-orbit coupling in conjunction with an external magnetic field can create a effective field orthogonal to it, beneficial for promoting superconductivity. However, this side coupling also has the potential to destroy it. This work promotes a theoretical model for a system with Rashba spin-orbit coupling, outer magnetic field and pairing interactions. Under the mean-field approximation, our model can be used to obtain the ground-state energy and order parameter. To simplify the model's Hamiltonian for numerical calculations, an new type of unitary transformation is used that takes the Rashba side coupling into account. By setting specific values for the model's parameters, we demonstrate that the transformation successfully promotes the side coupling and promotes superconductivity.

This study addresses the emerging area of verifying factual assertions about tabular datasets, a domain that has received relatively little attention. We propose a novel framework for validating factual statements concerning tabular data, where the framework is divided into two distinct components: identifying the attribute central to the assertion and determining its relevance in light of available evidence. The evidence comprises a selected key characteristic related to the asserted attribute. We further introduce a dataset comprising tabular entries and associated entries for both key characteristics and factual assertions. The resulting benchmark enables the evaluation of models' capabilities in performing characteristic verification and ultimate verification.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or metric dimension of G, denoted dim(G). Here, we introduce the idea of the k-point identifying dimension, written as dim_k(G), which is the smallest set of points that can uniquely identify every point in G up to an error of k. In this study, we define k-point identifying dominating sets and focus on finding G where dim_k(G) is at most n/G, with n being the total number of points in G. To achieve this, we use a combination of a random graph model and a greedy algorithm to find a solution.

The movement of groundwater in expansive areas is largely governed by the Darcy equation. In this study, we've developed a novel approach to modeling groundwater flow over vast distances. Our method combines the spectral element technique with techniques from numerical analysis. By utilizing high-order continuous functions in space and continuous discontinuous functions temporally, we've created a continuous-discontinuous spectral element method. This approach seamlessly bridges various time and space scales, allowing us to simulate groundwater flow at a spectral accuracy. Our technique's flexibility in spatial and temporal discretization provides us with the ability to optimize computational resources. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through a case study involving groundwater flow across a vast geographic area. Our simulation accurately reproduces the groundwater flow patterns and levels observed in the study area, validating our approach.

A novel, energy-efficient air purifying system utilizes the combination of ultraviolet and oxygen to create environmentally friendly ozone, which effectively oxidizes pollutants in a compact setup. The system's performance was studied using a numerical simulation that accounted for chemical reactions and heat transfer. The results showed that adding UV radiation and controlling the zone of intense reactions improved the efficiency of pollutant removal. The simulation also revealed an optimal balance between pollutant removal and heat generation, with non-dimensional heat values ranging from 0.01 to 0.1. The study found that increasing the number of reaction zones and optimizing flow patterns led to higher pollutant removal rates, reaching up to 95% under favorable conditions.

Esperanto, a Python-based simulation tool, is designed for evaluating neuromorphic computing systems based on event-driven architectures. The latest update to Esperanto enables event-driven simulation across multiple core simulations, leveraging the event-queue based approach of common C++ based simulators like SpiNNaker, enabling efficient use of available hardware resources and reducing simulation times. Furthermore, a new event type has been added to facilitate direct communication between core simulations, bypassing the need for inter-core neural message transmission. New classes for modeling neurons and synapses have been developed to take advantage of these features, and additional support has been added for hardware-specific models and the NEF neuron model.

To address the challenge of reducing reliance on untrustworthy black-box models, we introduce a modification to the standard Decision Tree algorithm, resulting in the Indecision Tree. This updated algorithm allocates more data points to leaf nodes, enhancing model transparency while maintaining comparable prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the Indecision Tree can be combined with active learning for efficient use of limited labeled data. Our experiments reveal that the Indecision Tree not only handles uncertainty better than its traditional counterpart but also outperforms the Bayesian Network in similar situations.

DTW-based algorithms are commonly applied in various fields, such as speech recognition, gesture recognition, and similar tasks. However, these algorithms can be computationally intensive and often require significant simplifications to function in real-time. We've developed a new approach that enables DBSCAN-based clustering to operate at a single data point at a time, significantly enhancing its scalability. Furthermore, we've created an innovative DTW algorithm, called EAPrunedDTW, which offers precomputed and postcomputed optimizations to accelerate DTW calculations. By incorporating these optimizations, our approach significantly outperforms existing methods, including Self-Aligning DTW and DTW-Edit, in terms of speed, while still achieving similar levels of accuracy.

This paper outlines our strategy for engaging students in testing concepts through a virtual, interactive approach. By incorporating multiple, context-driven methods to demonstrate the significance of testing, we aim to inspire students to actively participate and think critically. Our methods can be applied in various forms - either as a single activity within a lecture or as a comprehensive framework - and we provide the freedom for instructors to tailor their presentations to their specific needs. We also explore the benefits and challenges of using technology to enhance testing education and invite researchers to contribute by sharing their experiences and insights in this area.

In domains such as healthcare and law, where trust and transparency are crucial, explainable AI is becoming increasingly important. However, current visualization methods for black-box models' decision-making processes are often inaccessible due to their technical complexity. This has led to a need for more user-friendly visualization tools that can cater to non-expert users. A groundbreaking study pioneers the creation of a virtual reality interface for viewing and interacting with attention maps on complex 3D objects, allowing for hands-free exploration and manipulation of their different facets.

Over-smoothing significantly hinders the effectiveness of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), making them converge to a single state. Although various techniques have been developed to address this issue, most involve heuristic assumptions. In this research, we develop a theoretical framework to explain over-smoothing, identifying the root cause as the difficulty in GCNs from the perspective of optimization. Building on this understanding, we propose Optimal Propagation GCN (OP-GCN), a novel architecture designed to overcome this limitation. By incorporating a graph structure learning module and an adaptive learning rate method, OP-GCN enables the model to converge to an optimal solution. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that OP-GCN outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, particularly in scenarios involving large networks or high hop distances.

A search for invisible decays of the Z boson and the production of mono-z jets is presented. This investigation utilizes data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS experiment in 2016, totaling 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data. Data analysis involves examining final states containing leptons and jets, alongside missing transverse momentum. No data excess over standard predictions was observed. Direct constraints on the simple rho-model of dark matter particles were obtained, with contact interactions of the force-carrying particle X having an optimal coupling constant of approximately 0.3 GeV$^{-2}$. Additionally, the study provides limits on the GUT-scale fermion-fermion-scalars interaction, with a optimal scalar-fermion-fermion coupling constant of approximately 10$^{-5}$ GeV$^{-1}$.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are directly related to quark spin orientation, and we examine their implications within the context of the Wigner distribution framework.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the property that these two definitions yield the same topological space.

The synthesis of Heusler compounds via the molecular beam epitaxy technique is widely used.  When grown on a substrate, these compounds' atomic arrangement is influenced by the substrate's crystal structure.  In our study, we observed an unexpected phenomenon where a disordered Heusler compound, initially grown on graphene, formed an ordered phase after transferring to a new substrate.  By examining the compound using X-ray diffraction and scanning tunneling microscopy, we found that it had developed a crystalline structure with a specific atomic arrangement.  This new ordered phase has a atomic arrangement that matches the underlying graphene substrate's atomic arrangement.  This phenomenon, where the atomic arrangement of the compound is influenced by the atomic arrangement of the substrate, has also been observed in other materials.  To understand the conditions necessary for remote epitaxy, we conducted simulations and found that disordered compounds with a specific atomic arrangement can develop an ordered arrangement when they have a specific atomic arrangement.  This suggests that disordered Heusler compounds can be used to create ordered materials.

We introduce a new approach to identifying the ranks of time series that exhibit random patterns, particularly in situations where traditional methods are not applicable due to large amounts of data or insufficient information. This method relies on the stability of eigenvalues in an adjusted version of the sample covariance matrix that accounts for common trends in time series. A theoretical analysis shows that key stability measures for these eigenvalues can provide a consistent estimate of the random pattern ranks as data increases. A method is developed to determine the ranks of these matrices based on eigenvalues and this method is proven to converge to the true ranks in the long run. This method is then applied to time series analysis in a way that generalizes existing approaches, particularly in forecasting, while offering improvements that reduce bias and enhance accuracy.

Recent observations using the VLT/MUSE, which revealed a highly magnified galaxy associated with the galaxy cluster Abell 370, paved the way for a deeper analysis following a subsequent discovery of multiple images of another highly magnified galaxy within the same field of view using the JWST. By combining these observations with a model of the MUSE data, a preliminary estimate of the galaxy's redshift and physical properties was obtained, revealing that it is likely a massive galaxy at a redshift of approximately 3.5 with an estimated mass of around 10 to the power of 11 solar masses. Although further verification of the redshift is necessary, the galaxy's properties are consistent with a rare, massive galaxy that has been significantly magnified by the MUSE's powerful telescope.

Internet Service Providers (ISPs) are considering profit-sharing agreements with
content providers to improve their online services. In this paper, we examine such
arrangements by analyzing how quality-of-service enhancements and related cost
affect the agreements. We develop profit-sharing formulas that are feasible to
implement, and find that appropriate sharing can maximize profits for both parties.
Our research reveals profit-sharing's ability to incentivize ISPs to provide high
quality, and in turn, increase demand for the content provider's services.

The GNS construction forms states on a *C*-algebra into equivalent *-representations on a Hilbert space. For any -morphism between two *C*-algebras with respective states, we prove that associated Hilbert spaces and *-representations are unitarily equivalent under certain conditions. This leads to the demonstration that Hilbert spaces from GNS construction using states on a *C*-algebra, whose associated *-representations are irreducible and weakly faithful Hilbert spaces.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory are known for being consistent with current observations, and have the potential to be distinguished through future studies. The effect of introducing an arbitrary non-Gaussianity parameter in a specific axion model based on the sine-Lyth model is investigated. The introduction of this parameter significantly alters the model's non-Gaussianity and observability, and may render it unobservable with future forecasts. The space of $\alpha$-attractor models is further explored, and a comprehensive set of parameters is developed to describe this space. The resulting parameter space is found to be largely unaffected by the introduction of non-Gaussianity, and is found to be almost entirely consistent with current observations, and likely to be further supported by future observations.

The set of measured foliations on a given topological type of Riemann surface forms a convex cone with a topological characterization that's invariant under homeomorphisms. When mapping this type of surface onto another, measured foliations on the target's Riemann surface are in one-to-one correspondence with the foliations that result from pushing forward the surface map, forming a subset within the foliations' convex cone on the target. Specifically, if the target surface is part of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifold structure, its Fuchsian components are found at the vertices of a polygon in the surface' Teichmüller space. We have developed an explicit method for finding this set of foliations that correspond to these Fuchsian components, and used it to create new hyperbolic 3-manifolds with specific properties, including those that are not Haken.

This paper develops a mathematical framework for multi-currency portfolio analysis, enabling the calculation of portfolio yields in multiple currencies and their corresponding YTM distributions. Building upon previous work by Kahl and Timmermann, we extend their results to accommodate multiple currencies, and derive formulas for calculating key risk metrics such as Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk. Our framework also provides a means for the flexible pricing of portfolio-contingent derivatives.

Early detection of heart conditions through cardiac auscultation enables timely diagnosis and prevents severe heart attacks. The resulting stethoscope sounds offer valuable diagnostic clues, yet listening to them can be challenging due to background noise. This study presents a cardiac sound classification framework based on deep learning that categorizes chest sounds as normal or abnormal. We employed a pre-trained AlexNet model on 3700 heart sound clips from the KDD'19 dataset, achieving exceptional outcomes with 98.5% accuracy, 98.4% precision, 98.5% recall, and 98.5% F1 score after fine-tuning on the KNN classifier. This approach achieved superior performance compared to existing methods, marking significant advancements in cardiac sound classification.

In a 2001 study, we calculated the $s$-$p$ PV transition amplitude in C$^+$ using a relativistic no-core shell model, and used it to calculate the longitudinal PV Stark shift in $^{17}$O$+$ C$^+$. A subsequent study in 2014 calculated the Stark shift in $^{22}$Ne C$^+$, and an experiment was conducted to measure the PV effect in this atom. The results of the 2014 calculation showed disagreement with a 2001 prediction, and an experiment measuring the PV effect in Sc$^+$ is currently ongoing.

We identify twists in the framework of topological $K$-theory up to weak equivalence, classifying them within the group cohomology structure $H^1_{\text{coc}}(G, \underline{\mathbb{R}}/ \underline{\mathbb{Z}})$. Our findings extend prior work by D. Blaszczyk et al. and demonstrate that the earlier results of A. Rosenberg and S. Ma\'zur on the triviality of induced cohomology classes align with our established outcomes.

To effectively address the underrepresentation of diverse groups in educational
and technological fields, a remediative approach is insufficient. Instead, anti-
deficit methods that focus on leveraging diverse backgrounds are necessary.
This study explores the experiences of women in computer engineering through in-depth
interviews, highlighting the importance of institutional support in fostering
diversity. A remediative method of recruiting and training women is only effective
when combined with anti-deficit strategies that involve fostering a diverse student
body, inclusive teaching methods, and a supportive institutional environment.

We examine the boundedness of the fractional sum operator on fractional spaces and
subspaces of these spaces. Specifically, if parameters satisfy certain conditions,
the operator is bounded from $H^p(Z)$ to $\ell^q(Z)$ and from $H^p(Z)$ to $L^q(Z)$.
These conditions are optimal and we also investigate the boundedness of the fractional
sum operator and the difference operator on homogeneous Besov spaces.

The role of auction integrity on bidding behavior and revenue implications is examined through a study on two types of auctions - a confidential auction and a transparent reverse auction - in a setting with multiple item purchases from numerous suppliers. We found that while each format has situations in which it is optimal for the buyer, each also has scenarios in which the buyer may be misled by the auction they choose. The buyer's revenue can be significantly higher in the transparent auction compared to the confidential one, but this is not always the case. The degree of supplier heterogeneity influences this dynamic, with more diverse suppliers generally leading to the transparent auction yielding more revenue, except when demand in the confidential auction is very high.

The research focuses on gravity theories based on Weitzenbock geometry, which lack the non-metricity scalar, typically associated with $f(T)$ theories that assume geodesic completeness. To address this, we examine a specific transformation of the vierbein, corresponding to coordinate changes, and its impact on the action and equations of motion. Although the modified theory's equations bear resemblance to General Relativity, we identify critical discrepancies in the configuration space, ultimately finding that the transformation trivially modifies the theory, rendering it equivalent to General Relativity without any novel features.

We establish a structure theorem for locally defined ideals of Hessenberg varieties,
which are subspaces of Flag varieties associated with endomorphisms having specific
permutation patterns. 
Using this theorem, we can approximate the full I-adic algebra of D-module sections of
Hessenberg varieties by its localized counterparts, which are easier to compute. 
This result has significant implications for the study of chromatic symmetric functions of
line graphs associated with rooted trees, as it allows us to express the chromatic
symmetric functions in terms of the local cohomology of the localized cohomology rings.

Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, can generate brushstrokes that mimic the style of various artists. However, training these neural painters from scratch is both time-consuming and resource-intensive. To overcome these limitations, we propose employing a specific rendering technique that enables training on a broader range of artworks. Our framework, built upon existing style-transfer models, can be adapted to create neural painters capable of producing high-quality brushstrokes. To validate our approach, we demonstrate its effectiveness in replicating specific artistic styles, such as Van Gogh's, across various complex scenes. Our method, in comparison to existing techniques, achieves superior results in capturing the nuances of Van Gogh's style while also maintaining a lower level of contamination.

The key components of the New Physics case for the coming generation of experiments are outlined, with a particular emphasis on the role that the LHC will play in this context. Several specific examples of such a case have been put forward, with one such instance being the CP-violating Kaon decay. This particular decay offers the distinct advantage of requiring only one loop to occur and is notably insensitive to New Physics that may have occurred at high energy scales. The proposed solution to this challenge involves the introduction of a new, heavy gauge boson known as the Z'. The Z' is suggested to contribute to the decay of the Kaon through its vector-like quark Z' coupling. The Z' can also be created in high-energy proton-proton collisions, with the potential to be discovered at the LHC, particularly given its potentially large kinematic signature. The proposed solution to this challenge involves the vector-like quark Z' coupling to fermions.

Academic researchers have developed vast collections of references, but the knowledge within them remains largely underutilized by the general public. To make research more accessible, researchers have created preprints that provide easy-to-understand summaries. PreprintAnnotate is an innovative system that automatically creates detailed annotations for these summaries by analyzing the corresponding research papers. PreprintAnnotate's process involves three main steps: extracting key concepts from the papers, linking these concepts to a knowledge base, and using the information to answer detailed questions about the papers. This system then generates comprehensive annotations for the summaries. To verify its accuracy, the system was tested on 18,000 annotations related to 1,200 machine learning preprints, achieving a high F1 score of 0.862.

In core-collapse supernovae, the rapid oscillation of neutrinos is thought to occur due to an imbalance in the rates at which they change flavors, influenced by the density of neutrinos and electrons. This density-dependent process takes place within the region where the infalling material meets the outwardly moving shockwave. Core-collapse supernovae in eight different three-dimensional simulations were analyzed to determine the conditions that support this phenomenon. These conditions include a wide range of stellar masses and explosion mechanisms. This analysis focused on the characteristics of the region where the shockwave meets the infalling material, including its size, density, and composition. This research found that all the simulations were able to support the density required for the density-dependent process to occur, although some of them did not have enough low-mass nuclei to support the momentum exchange required for the instability to occur. This research found that the mass of the star, the rotation of the star, and the magnetic field of the star all affect the region where the density-dependent process is most active. This research found that more massive stars have smaller regions of low-mass nuclei, while faster rotation and stronger magnetic fields result in larger regions of instability. This research found that the density-dependent process is most active in certain types of supernovae, including those that do not explode due to the fallback of mass.

In this research, we introduce a novel deep learning model for accurately diagnosing ADHD by leveraging convolutional neural networks that utilize pre-processed functional MRI data. By focusing on key anatomical brain areas, we enhance both computational efficiency and model interpretability. Additionally, our model employs a multi-layer approach that utilizes shared and specific features of these regions, ultimately yielding superior diagnostic results compared to using comprehensive MRI data or simplified models.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where the population is divided into equal-sized compartments, we analyze an scenario with a Moore neighbourhood connectivity pattern. Our model assumes that a certain percentage of susceptible individuals interact with infectives from neighbouring compartments, leading to potential infection. Similarly, we consider that susceptible individuals can recover when interacting with recoverers, and infectives can recover when interacting with recoverers, with the probabilities of these processes governed by constants. We determine the conditions under which an endemic equilibrium exists in the interior of the model's state space, obtaining a precise formula for this equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish the global stability of this equilibrium using refined analysis techniques, and our results can be applied to more complex models with connectivity matrices that have non-negative entries.

Acronyms are widely used in written texts due to their ability to save space and convey information efficiently. However, their ambiguous nature can lead to confusion and hinder text comprehension. To address this issue, our research focuses on providing clear acronyms by utilizing contextual information. By analyzing the full forms and associated acronyms within their respective contexts, our system can make informed decisions and supply users with the most suitable full form. Our approach relies on a deep learning-based, unsupervised model that analyzes the semantic relationships between potential full forms and acronym texts, taking into consideration the surrounding words. This model, built using word embeddings, outperforms existing methods and demonstrates significant improvements over the best available solutions.

Quantum interference significantly impacts the behavior of thermoelectric currents.
Consequently, these currents exhibit distinct patterns resulting from constructive
and destructive interference. To better understand this phenomenon, we examine
thermoelectric currents flowing through identical parallel quantum systems under
two scenarios: when thermoelectric currents are influenced solely by interference
among charges, and when they are affected by interactions between charges and
thermal fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that while thermoelectric currents
can be completely suppressed in the absence of interaction through selective
phase tuning, they cannot be completely suppressed when interaction takes place.
Moreover, interaction gives rise to thermoelectric currents characterized by
distinct patterns of superposition and conditional probability.

Our proposed DNA-storage system utilizes a unique data structure based on the $k$-mer concept, allowing random access and efficient data updates, which were previously challenging with existing DNA-storage methods. Our architecture's hierarchical organization of data into multiple levels, from chromosomes to addresses, facilitates simple pointer updates for replacing data, resulting in significant reductions in biological costs. Our simulations demonstrate that the overhead of these pointer updates is minimal, with less than a 2% increase in costs for frequent updates, making the architecture highly suitable for applications that involve frequent data updates. Our extensive experiments using real-world datasets, including Wikipedia and LogMine, show that our architecture achieves substantial DNA-efficiencies of up to 1000 times the baseline, with additional advantages of fast search operations and no decrease in capacity due to such storage.

Research on condensed matter has uncovered exotic materials with unique transport properties, such as quantum Hall and valence-hall insulators. To further our understanding of insulating materials, we investigate theoretically whether a new class of insulators, characterized by mixed-anomaly and possessing both Hall and relaxed-junction junctions, could exist in two-dimensional systems with time-reversal symmetry. In this study, we examine whether a specific arrangement of layers can create a promising candidate for such a new insulator at its boundary.

In oscillatory media, regions with accelerated oscillation frequencies can influence synchronization across entire systems, regardless of their spatial confinement.  This phenomenon is particularly evident in biological systems, where pacemaker-generated waves spread through reentrant waves and synchronize distant areas of the heart, leading to arrhythmias.  To better understand this process, researchers have developed a sophisticated mathematical model that simulates the behavior of an elastic, viscoelastic, and inelastic membrane, which is a fundamental aspect of mechanical hyperpolarization.  This model, when applied to the Cahn-Scott phase-field model, reveals that viscoelastic effects have a significant impact on the membrane's response to pacemaker-generated stimuli.  Specifically, the membrane becomes more responsive to these stimuli when viscoelastic effects are present, and the resulting deformation patterns are influenced by factors such as membrane tension and relaxation times.  These findings have important implications for our understanding of mechanical hyperpolarization and its potential role in cellular processes.

A connection between quantum algorithms and entropy is established, specifically between complexity and the approximation of Shannon and von Neumann entropies for random variables and mixed-state density matrices. We define a general class of distributions and demonstrate that its entropy can be complexitarily defined. Our findings indicate that approximating the Shannon entropy of a random variable or the von Neumann entropy of a mixed-state density matrix within polynomial relative error polynomial relative to the entropy value itself requires polynomial quantum queries. Under certain conditions, such as when approximating the entropy to a polynomial relative error without prior knowledge of the entropy value, approximating the entropy polynomial times log n quantum queries is possible. We also examine the case of approximating Renyi entropies and prove that calculating Renyi entropies with relative error approximations polynomial relative to the index s and the inverse of Renyi entropy value s^{-1} E_{s+1}^{-1}(X) requires n^{2s} quantum queries.

The widespread adoption of AI across various sectors necessitates a substantial database to support its development, requiring a considerable investment of resources. A resource-efficient data acquisition approach is developed, leveraging the Internet of Things (IoT) to gather diverse, real-time multimedia data from everyday devices. This data is then applied to enhance AI capabilities in real-world scenarios, specifically to improve face-based emotion recognition. A novel system is designed to analyze the video feeds from smartphones to accurately categorize adult emotions. The system utilizes a real-time face detection algorithm and a mobile application to simplify interaction, allowing users to convey their emotions through a game-like interface. The data collected using this approach demonstrates promising outcomes in initial trials, showcasing the feasibility of the proposed solution.

Physicians' written assessments of patients' symptoms and history are referred to as clinical text notes. These notes, which are part of electronic health records, are utilized by medical professionals to make diagnoses and treatment plans. Although NLP-based tools are becoming more prevalent in clinical settings, their implementation in practice remains limited. In order to facilitate automated diagnosis and treatment recommendations, ICD coding involves categorizing clinical text notes according to specific disease patterns. In this study, we present the first open competition for Indonesian ICD coding, aiming to enhance the availability of NLP research in Indonesian. To support this initiative, we have developed and introduced a new dataset consisting of 10,122 clinical text notes, each annotated with up to five corresponding ICD codes.
