This paper re-evaluates the role of Monitoring as a fundamental concept in real-time system oversight and development. By leveraging Monitoring's properties in defining the monitoring condition and constructing the monitoring model, the practical applications of defining monitoring conditions and building observation models are simplified and enhanced. To achieve this, we incorporate the Metric Interval Temporal Logic into the monitoring condition and develop a corresponding metric interval logic for the monitoring model. In order to automate the construction of the monitoring model, we develop a method that utilizes the pre-existing system model, which can be expressed in either a discrete-time or continuous-time transition system. Our method involves translating the monitoring condition into a non-deterministic finite automaton, then merging it with the system model to generate the monitoring model, which can also be expressed as a non-deterministic finite automaton. Through case studies, we showcase the practical value of our technique in simplifying the construction of the monitoring model.

The breaking of isospin symmetry in meson-meson transitions is primarily driven by
mass differences between up and down quarks, resulting in transitions involving
different mesets through intermediate processes that respect isospin symmetry.
Consequently, the discrepancies between experiment and theory regarding branching
ratios for channels involving identical versus non-identical mesets can be accounted
for without resorting to electromagnetic interactions.

The main camera on the ESO Very Large Telescope Interferometer, called the Acquisition Camera, has played a crucial role in the instrument's operations since its installation in 2014. This camera's operations have been improved with the release of the latest software version, QBI v6.3, which offers enhanced functionality and easier access to its features. This article details the capabilities of the Acquisition Camera and provides a guide for its operations following the recent software upgrade.

We examine the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem in the context of r being a maximum distance parameter, and d being a maximum degree parameter for the input graph G. Our main finding is that for any given epsilon, we can devise a scheme to approximate the problem within (1 + epsilon) accuracy in polynomial time relative to r and exponential time relative to d and log r. This involves creating two separate algorithms to handle different scenarios based on the value of r in relation to d.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $P\left(\frac{f(q^c \cdot z)}{f(z) + Q(z)}\right) = 0$ resides within the class $S_{\rho_2}^{\cl}$, with the hyper-order not exceeding $\max\{\rho_P, \rho_{exp}, \rho_Q\\}$, where $\rho_{exp}$ is the exponential order of $e^{Q(z)}$, and $\rho_P$, $\rho_Q$ are the orders of polynomials $P$ and $Q$. Furthermore, under specific conditions, the hyper-order of these solutions exactly matches the degree of the polynomial $Q$. This finding extends and supersedes previous outcomes from multiple researchers, including Lins-Souza, Heibutzki, and others, while also addressing outcomes from multiple authors, including Li, Yang, and others, as well as the work of Chen and Kong.

This research focuses on efficiently solving polynomial linear systems of size n x n that may contain errors, over a finite field of size q. We present an approach that transforms these systems into error-free polynomial diagonal systems of size 2n x 2n, which can then be solved using a combination of a novel direct solver and an established solver for Kaltofen's matrix. Our method requires O(ñ^ω log n + ñ^ω log q) operations, where ñ is a value proportional to the size of the system and ω is the matrix multiplication exponent. This approach matches the efficiency of established iterative methods in terms of asymptotic complexity and often performs better in practice.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime, we examine a two-photon interaction between a quantum harmonic oscillator and a binary quantum emitter. To achieve accurate modeling, operator-dressed methods are applied to avoid erroneous conclusions. For emitter types with even parity, we discover an exactly solvable two-phancer oscillator, yielding a complete set of eigenstates and energies. Conversely, in cases involving odd parity, the light-matter interaction exhibits strict photon emission restrictions, permitting only pairs of photons to be emitted. By exploring the system's steady-state light scattering, we demonstrate the ability to manipulate quantum correlations between emitted photons, thereby enhancing their suitability for use in single-photon switching and entanglement purposes.

A new analytical equation of state for the isentrope of pure alkali metals has been derived and verified by comparing it to the results of ab initio calculations across the entire pressure range from 0 to 200 Mbar. Based on this equation of state, key thermodynamic properties such as pressure, bulk modulus, and adiabatic index have been calculated and plotted against pressure. Furthermore, this equation of state has been used to create approximate expressions for the adiabatic and Gruneisen equations of state applicable to the entire pressure range. Using these derived equations of state, shock Hugoniot curves for sodium, potassium, and rubidium have been generated and will be used in future research to model the dynamic compression of astrophysical objects, including brown dwarfs and gas giant planets.

In the context of vector meson dominance model, we've established a framework for vector mesons in local Lorentz invariant form, allowing us to derive a simplified equation for vector mesons within a vector dominance model framework, accounting for chiral imbalance. As a result, we found that vector mesons are unaffected by the CHDM but their mass and decay widths are influenced. Furthermore, we found that the form factors of vector mesons are affected by the CHDM and depend on the momentum of the vector mesons.

We've developed a distributed algorithm for nodes in a network to synchronize their states despite the influence of malicious nodes. Our solution can handle a large network of nodes and multiple layers of influence from malicious nodes. We've designed it to be adaptable to networks with multiple layers and able to handle multiple rounds of updates. Our algorithm was tested in simulations and found to be able to handle multiple layers of malicious nodes up to a certain depth in the network.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter setups, such as infalling matter from multiple directions, it is essential to solve the Hamiltonian constraint at the start to ensure that an initial data set can be used. We have developed a method to solve this constraint by combining it with a modified version of the momentum constraint, which we call the Lapse Equation. By doing so, we can avoid solving the full elliptic system of equations for the Lapse and Radial gauge, which was a major limitation of our previous approach. Instead, we only need to solve for these variables in the region where the constraint equations apply, making our method more efficient. Although there are some challenges with this new constraint formulation, such as ensuring smoothness at certain points, it has been shown to produce satisfactory results in various scenarios.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment is to investigate neutrino oscillations with high precision through a large-scale, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector. This detector will be situated 53-73 km away from two nuclear power plants in southern China, where it will also analyze the reactor antineutrino spectrum to resolve an ongoing controversy. In this analysis of a 2021 J. Phys. G article, researchers discuss the progress of the experiment's construction as of 2021, including the status of the detector's support structures, the purification of the target volume's water, and the ongoing data-taking and analysis processes.

Time-series data analysis has been a significant area of study for
statisticians and computer scientists for an extended period, with applications
ranging from economics to power systems. Long sequence time-series forecasting
is particularly crucial in scenarios such as power systems and climate change
research. In this research, we address the problem of long sequence forecasting
for multivariate time-series by developing a novel model, long-term
Transformer (longformer), which is an extension of the existing Transformer
model. longformer is designed to effectively capture long-range dependencies
in time-series data by introducing additional mechanisms, including time-aware
masking, an efficient decoder, and an innovative attention initialization
method. Our experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that longformer
outperforms existing advanced models in terms of forecasting accuracy,

Astronomical observations using a spectrograph are limited by dispersion, which can be mitigated with an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC). The effectiveness of our new, low-cost dual-prism ADC design was tested with a 0.35m telescope at the Paranal Observatory, and the results showed that the ADC's performance matches or exceeds that of high-end commercial models, particularly at shorter wavelengths and shorter dispersions. The cost-efficiency of the ADC makes it accessible for smaller telescopes.

Recently, pre-trained models have shown great potential in ranking tasks, 
however, they often require significant computational resources. To address this issue, 
knowledge distillation has been proposed as an effective method to enhance ranking models. 
Building on this concept, we introduce a new approach that leverages language models 
to provide contextualized word meanings and relevance signals. This method involves 
creating a dummy query by concatenating all terms in a document and then using a 
language model to evaluate its potential relevance. The output from this process 
is then used to train a simple cross-encoder model. We also propose a novel 
training strategy that utilizes multiple documents per sample to optimize our 
cross-encoder model. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, 
which achieves notable improvements over existing methods and produces models that 
offer a practical balance between performance and resource efficiency.

Bosonic dark matter with ultra-light mass can be detected through its wave-like properties, producing oscillating electric and gravitational fields. This signal has two components, and while researchers have focused on its oscillating nature, we propose an alternative approach. We demonstrate that integrating the oscillating signal over time yields a non-zero, frequency-dependent residual signal. This new approach offers a more comprehensive understanding of detector responses and could enhance detector design and data analysis methods. We also present a novel detection strategy that focuses on establishing a confidence interval for this residual signal, providing researchers with an additional tool in their search for this specific type of dark matter.

This paper focuses on the inverse problem of determining a one-dimensional Radon measure from the low-frequency Fourier coefficients of its convolution with a known $L^1$-function. We investigate whether a solution exists and, if so, is it unique? We establish criteria for the uniqueness of such a solution and provide sufficient conditions for its existence. These conditions are expressed in terms of a specific linear operator's properties, specifically its injectivity and the finite dimensionality of its kernel.

P4, a programming language for customizable switches, has numerous implementations
known as devices, but the relationship between software and hardware in terms of
performance and correctness remains unclear. A new tool called Validation Assistant
(VN) has been developed to bridge this knowledge gap. VN takes two P4 programs as
input, one for each, and compares their behavior to determine if they are equivalent
or to identify differences in correctness and performance. Using an abstract
interpreter, VN automatically analyzes the programs and can verify their equivalence
by proving that their outputs match, or explain discrepancies in how they behave.
A key innovation is the use of specialized data structures that mimic the actual
switches, allowing VN to precisely measure program performance and to verify that
similar inputs produce identical results in similar time frames. Through testing with
real-world P4 programs, VN has shown its ability to verify program equivalence in
various scenarios and to confirm that some programs perform consistently across
different hardware implementations.

In numerical simulations of fluid flow, a common task involves resolving the vector transport equation, where the velocity field is assumed to be known and smooth. Although standard methods often treat this assumption as valid, they typically use a basic discretization approach, leading to an inaccurate representation of the smooth velocity field. In contrast, we propose treating the velocity field with a more sophisticated discretization, which better reflects its smoothness, and show that doing so allows us to develop more efficient and accurate solution methods, ultimately enabling direct solution schemes that bypass iterative processes.

The rapid advancement of deep learning has led to widespread adoption across various sectors, despite concerns regarding ethical implications such as privacy and security risks. To address these issues, a thorough examination of the ethical concerns surrounding deep learning is presented, along with a detailed analysis of how deep learning technologies impact privacy and security. Furthermore, potential solutions are proposed to mitigate these concerns.

Scientists have analyzed data collected by the LHCb experiment, totaling 90 million $B_c^+$ ions and 96 million $B_c^- ions$, to identify the $B_{0s}^{(3)}$ state of $B_c^+$. The analysis revealed two distinct peaks, indicating a new excited state of $B_c^+$. The masses of these peaks correspond to $10852.3 \pm 0.6$ (statistical error) $\pm 1.0$ (systematic error) MeV/$c^2$ and $10864.4 \pm 0.7$ (statistical error) $\pm 1.0$ (systematic error) MeV/$c^2$, and the spins of these peaks are believed to be $1$ and $2$, respectively.

In the early 1990s, Symes and McLaughlin developed Heterogeneous Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods, now referred to as HHBVM, which are a specific type of numerical method that combine function evaluation with Hamiltonian system solutions in a boundary context. These methods are characterized by their ability to preserve energy exactly in theory, although this exact preservation is compromised in practical applications due to floating-point arithmetic limitations. Our research aims to address this discrepancy by developing a more accurate computational framework that allows HHBVM to maintain precise energy conservation, thereby enhancing their applicability to problems requiring high levels of accuracy and long-term stability.

To enhance neural network performance without increasing its size, we can update 
specific layers collectively using localized feedback from critic networks that track 
the progress of these groups. By implementing this strategy, we can optimize 
computational efficiency and memory usage, allowing for broader updates of layers 
without incurring additional costs. Our approach features critic networks with 
similar architectures to their corresponding localized forward passes, enabling 
training at optimized resource costs. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness 
of this method in solving complex problems like the Travelling Salesman problem and 
in training neural networks to play games like Atari games.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has historically been understudied compared to its two-dimensional counterpart. We have developed an innovative numerical framework for calculating three-dimensional scattering phase coherence residues and applied it to analyze the topological structure of coherent regions in scattering processes. Our research focuses on a three-dimensional billiard system featuring two intersecting cylindrical components, one of which can be rotated to create various boundary configurations. We observed that, unlike similar systems in two dimensions, three-dimensional non-Wada domains transition smoothly into Wada domains with the introduction of weak dissipation.

A groundbreaking discovery in particle physics, the $e^+e^-\to \tau \tau \gamma$ reaction offers a unique opportunity to study an unusual interaction between $\tau$ leptons and $\gamma$ photons. The unusual lepton-photon interaction can distort the angular distribution of $\gamma$ photons produced in $e^+e^-\to \tau \tau \gamma$ reactions, resulting in $\gamma$ production and decay far apart in space and time. The occurrence of these $\gamma$ interactions can be detected through the separation of $\gamma$ production and decay points, as well as the time difference between them. The event selection criteria used to identify $\gamma$ interactions rely on the $\tau$ decay products and the $\gamma$ trajectory, resulting in the prediction of observable $\gamma$ interactions at the Belle II experiment with measurable prediction intervals.

Human action understanding in complex videos is crucial for various applications, yet currently, deep learning models struggle to effectively capture the structure and meaning of these videos. This research introduces the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), a novel deep learning model designed for understanding action meaning in videos with multiple segments. HAN incorporates two attention mechanisms to consider both local video structure and global sentence meaning. Empirical results on established benchmarks demonstrate the HAN's superiority in addressing action meaning extraction over existing methods.

Researchers have investigated the thermodynamic behaviors of extreme and over-extremal Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes in five dimensions.  By plotting the mass versus charge relationship for these black holes, we found that they intersect at a specific boundary defined by a non-zero horizon size.  This boundary signifies that naked singularities do not exist beyond it.  Our analysis also revealed that adiabatic processes cannot transform non-gravitational forces into gravitational ones in these black holes.  Furthermore, we found that both extreme and over-extremed black holes satisfy the weak, strong, and mixed forms of the Conjecture of Cosmic Censorship at points below the boundary, but at points on or above the boundary, these black holes can potentially violate the weak form of the Conjecture.

As star cluster forms, the process of star formation within the cluster is affected, ultimately impacting the process of planet formation. The process of planet formation, however, is a crucial component of the broader process of the universe's evolution. The study of the universe's evolution, therefore, must encompass the processes of star cluster formation, star formation, and planet formation. We suggest a method for employing entropy and mutual information from Shannon's theory to evaluate probability distributions and their associated random variables. 
This approach involves approximating Shannon's metrics with the Tsallis entropy and its related interaction information, which are simpler to calculate and do not require extensive data sets. 
Using the Fokker-Planck equation, we derive and apply a model for the time-dependent probability distribution of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. 
From this model, we compute the approximate entropy and mutual information at steady-state. 
As a result, we are able to derive the approximate Tsallis information at steady-state and explore its relationship with the proximity to Crisanti-Sommers line in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model.

In recent years, modeling of complex semiconductor manufacturing systems has received significant attention due to their wide application in the semiconductor industry. Researchers have explored various approaches to describe these systems using Partial Differential Equations and other methods, especially focusing on situations where particle velocities change abruptly, often resulting in shock waves. Our research focuses on solving mixed initial and free boundary value problems for the finite wave model in multiple spatial dimensions, where determining when and where new waves form poses a significant challenge. Our contribution involves developing precise predictions for the formation of shock waves, along with proving the existence and uniqueness of solutions under certain conditions, all while avoiding unnecessary assumptions in the model.

A company's cybersecurity is crucial to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive information, which can lead to significant financial loss and damage to reputation in case of a security breach. To protect against cyber threats, the company should adopt advanced detection methods such as using machine learning, along with cutting-edge encryption and firewalls. In this research, we focus on using the K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) algorithm to detect and prevent intrusion in wireless sensor networks. We simulate various types of attacks, including DoS and DDoS, and find that our approach effectively identifies and prevents these threats at a rate of 100%.

We have found a particular group, consisting of piecewise linear homeomorphisms, for which there exists a particular base point, such that the growth of the group when acting on that point exhibits a specific range of possible values for its growth rate.

The ability of animals to move through diverse environments is essential for
various activities, such as locating food, escaping from predators, and
reproducing. Animals' movement capabilities are limited by the physical
constraints of their body structures, which determine the range of movements
possible. In this research, a new method is proposed to analyze an animal's
movement potential by creating models that take into account their physical
constraints. This method involves developing simplified representations of
animals based on their movements, which can be used to predict their
locomotion capabilities.

This study focuses on optimizing overhead and underground transmission power networks by addressing the issue of excessive electricity surplus. To achieve this, we propose a method to determine the optimal placement and sizing of new transmission lines, which involves selecting underground locations to minimize land use and overhead locations to reduce power losses. Our approach formulates the problem as an optimization model that can be solved using genetic algorithms, and we validate its effectiveness through case analyses based on the Brazil South-West Power Interconnected System.

The emergence of machine learning and artificial intelligence has led to significant advancements in technology, yet it has also presented a new problem - the difficulty of using data-driven approaches to understand the physical laws governing the universe. Although existing data mining methods have achieved some success in specific areas, they often struggle to provide generalizable predictions beyond their respective fields. To address this challenge, we have developed a universal framework capable of identifying the underlying mathematical structures in diverse datasets, regardless of their origin. By applying our approach to various real-world datasets, we have demonstrated its potential to uncover and replicate complex relationships, even in the absence of prior knowledge.

This study introduces the concept of detectable, massive, long-lived particles that have significant mass and charge, and which are stable enough to be identified in experiments. These particles, often referred to as ROARs, can be found in experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) due to their unique signatures, which differ from those of standard model particles. In contrast to supersymmetric particles, which have been extensively searched for, LHC data has not yet provided definitive evidence for supersymmetry. However, LHC data does provide constraints on particles with similar characteristics, such as those found in dark matter research. A hypothetical detector at the LHC's interaction point can identify ROARs through the measurement of their ionization patterns and time of arrival, and in combination with data from other detectors, such as those in underground mines or in space, can provide a comprehensive understanding of dark matter and its relationship to supersymmetry.

We have developed a novel, compact and cost-effective single-photon source by integrating two layers of hexagonal nitride structures within a plasmonic cavity. The unique design features a highly reflective top layer and self-assembled quantum dots that generate photons in an ultra-narrow spectral range thanks to holey waveguides for filtering and spectroscopic analysis. Our innovative design enables a high Purcell factor and achieves Purcell-enhanced coupling of quantum dots to the cavity mode, resulting in a fast decay rate and high coupling efficiency. Our research has demonstrated a notable success in achieving rapid photon emission, with a notable reduction in decay time and high overall coupling efficiency.

In a recent study, researchers utilized terahertz spectroscopy to analyze the vibrational patterns near the boson peak of a glass made from borosilicate. By comparing the spectral density of vibrations to the generalized vibrational density of states, they found significant differences in the two measurements for this type of glass. Researchers theorized that these discrepancies arise from the distinct weighting given to low-frequency vibrations in their respective assessments. As a result, they proposed that employing normal mode analysis to analyze the borosilicate glass's structure revealed a connection between its macroscopic vibrational behavior and its underlying microscopic structure, specifically its structural relaxation time.

Particle physics theories rely heavily on precise calculations, specifically scattering cross sections, which are critical for predicting and interpreting experimental results. These cross sections require complex computations, such as calculating loop-scattering amplitudes, which are becoming increasingly difficult and demanding as the number of loops increases. This paper discusses the current status of loop amplitudes up to three loops and outlines strategies for tackling the computational challenges associated with these calculations.

In random systems, the concept of the deposition matrix is used to represent particle arrival rates, similar to the dose-rate, at various locations. Through numerical simulations, this study examines the DP matrix eigenvalue distribution and finds that it exhibits a pattern of following both the Porter-Thomas and chi-square distributions for its eigenvalue probability density, specifically for 1D and higher-dimensional cases. Additionally, it is observed that as system dimensionality increases, the dominant eigenvalue's relative importance decreases. In order to verify these results analytically, the deposition matrix is modeled in two scenarios - one where elements follow a Gaussian distribution and the other where elements follow a Poisson distribution. These model assessments show agreement with initial findings.

Researchers have observed the central region of our Galaxy, observing radio emissions from synchrotron sources. These sources are located in two distinct areas, referred to as the Near Arm and the Far Arm, separated by the Galactic plane. Despite similar electron densities in these regions, previous studies found significant differences in magnetic field strength. To investigate this, researchers conducted an analysis using data from the VLA and found that the difference between the two regions is likely not random, but rather the result of a physical process.

In recent years, quality diversity has gained attention as a means to discover a wide range of optimal behaviors in optimization problems, in contrast to methods that focus solely on finding the single best solution. Among the techniques that utilize quality diversity, the evolutionary multi-objective optimizer, or evolutionary behavior discovery framework, excels at finding diverse solutions to complex problems. However, the effectiveness of this method can be significantly impacted by its sensitivity to the dimensionality of the solutions it is optimizing. To overcome this limitation, we propose an approach that uses a mixtures of experts model to create an adaptable encoding system that can better handle high-dimensional adaptations. The results of our experiments show that this method can significantly improve diversity and convergence when compared to established approaches, particularly in finding solutions with the right number of components for multi-dimensional problems.

The Stable Roommates problem involves finding a stable pairing of agents with preferences for one another. A roommates object is a stable pairing that exists when one does. Researchers have discovered that objectivity or symmetry in preferences is essential for the existence of a stable pairing in multi-dimensional versions of the problem. Building on this discovery, we found that the existence of a stable pairing in the three-dimensional version of the problem can be determined by the presence of symmetry in its preferences. Our proof relies on converting a new category of games, which we called preference games, into tournaments. These games are defined by a preference relation that is both a majority and symmetric. Additionally, we found that the tournament derived from these games contains a Hamiltonian path that is both a majority and shortest.

The application of mechanical strain has been found to have significant effects on the properties of two-dimensional materials, particularly the valley Hall effect. We investigated how the application of strain affects the valley Hall coefficient in two types of materials, the AB phase of twisted bilayer graphene and twisted trilayer graphene. For twisted bilayer and trilayer graphene, the application of strain causes a non-linear decrease in the valley Hall angle, with strain also causing a shift in the valley Hall band extrema energy levels. Strain also causes a non-zero valley Hall angle in the valley Hall insulating phase, with this effect being particularly pronounced in the trilayer graphene under certain conditions.

We've developed a universal method to approximate the Gromov--Hausdorff distance, using a novel concept of cloud formation between metric spaces. Our approach is characterized by an optimal pair of functions, a small error value, and an approximate correspondence between the spaces within that error margin. The approximation can be further refined to achieve universal $\epsilon$-approximations for any given $\epsilon > 0$, resulting in polynomial-time construction methods. Our method is implemented in the Sycora framework, which is used to empirically evaluate the approximation quality against existing solutions.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna design is presented, operating at mm-wave frequencies with 28 GHz center frequency and 6.8 GHz bandwidth, featuring wide stopbands at 25-29 GHz and 35-39 GHz. It offers a high VSWR due to its large bandwidth, and incorporates two resonances for enhanced bandwidth. With an integrated ground shorting ring, the patch supports two fundamental modes at orthogonal frequencies, while a series-fed patch design provides an additional resonance, resulting in significant improvements. It features a compact size of 0.43λ x 0.4λ and high isolation between feed ports, and when integrated into an 8 x 8 array, it achieves 19.5 dBi gain with 100% aperture efficiency.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, necessitating a shift to moving-partitions syndrome extraction for hardware limitations. This paper explores the Measuring-Only surface code, an innovative approach that minimizes moving-parts operations by employing real-time measurements and Mølmer-Sørensen gates to entangle data and syndrome qubits. The research proposes a novel, efficient circuit design for implementing the Measuring-Only surface code, demonstrating its feasibility through simulations of potential near-term quantum devices.

Interferometry can be enhanced through quantum metrology by utilizing entangled states to achieve greater accuracy in measuring phase shifts.  A phase shift is crucial in determining astronomical object positions, and employing a quantum entangled state can lead to improved precision.  Researchers have developed methods to create these advanced states, and now explore a more efficient approach to generating this phase shift using a simpler form of entanglement.  This new approach involves using a pair of photons in an entangled state to produce the desired state with improved efficiency.  The experiment involves splitting a light beam and sending the resulting photons through a special optical setup that creates the desired entangled state.  The light beams are then split again, and the photons' phases are adjusted to produce the desired entangled state.  The experiment has shown that the new approach is more efficient than previous methods.

The PHENIX collaboration at RHIC has gathered data on direct photon-hadron correlations in Au+Au collisions at an energy of 200 GeV. They found that au+au collisions produce about half the number of photons per particle in comparison to pp collisions. However, they discovered that in Au+Au collisions, correlations of hadrons with high momentum (greater than 10 GeV/c) and low-momentum photons are more pronounced than in pp collisions. This suggests that high-energy quarks lose less energy when moving through the dense medium, whereas low-energy quarks lose more.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach, we utilize the continuous manipulation of qubit connectivity to emulate fermionic systems in first quantization. By aligning the connectivity with the Wigner-Weyl mapping, we can directly simulate fermionic interactions without needing to reorder fermions as is typically necessary in other methods. This connection allows us to reduce the complexity of simulating fermionic systems to that of interacting spinless particles, which can be further simplified under certain conditions. Our research indicates that for certain classes of fermionic wave functions, their effective dimension can increase significantly less than in other methods, thus reducing the computational resources required. We have developed and tested different connectivity structures to simulate a harmonic oscillator and the hydrogen atom, and found that the optimal connectivity should prioritize short-range interactions while also considering the spatial distribution of the particles. This approach has the potential to reduce the quantum resources required for simulating complex fermionic systems.

We introduce a novel technique for generating random networks with robust features, based on an advanced encoding method for multi-layered data, which allows for efficient optimization from the beginning and improved overall performance.

Achieving high efficiency in two-photon fluorescence microscopy in thick, scattering materials like the brain requires overcoming significant light loss obstacles. A solution to this problem involves using adaptive optics to correct for light loss, which increases its available intensity and penetration depth within such media. We have devised a technique that utilizes the localized fluorescence of spherical beads to map the optical transmission loss within brain tissue, which is then compensated for by adjusting a deformable mirror. We have applied this method to a study of the brain's blood vessels in mice, demonstrating its potential to overcome system efficiency limitations in the process.

Off-policy policy evaluation is often done using importance sampling, which can be very sensitive to large rewards and have a very high variance in off-policy data. However, it has been shown that if access to testing distribution data is available during training, an estimator called the direct estimator can be made very efficient. Although the direct estimator can be used on offline data, it needs access to testing distribution data at test time, which is not always available. In this paper, an alternative approach is proposed to train an approximator of the value function using the direct estimator on offline data, without needing testing distribution data at test time. The key innovation is an adaptive importance weighting scheme that assigns higher importance to data points that are more similar to the approximated value function, thus avoiding the need to assign equal importance to all data points as in the importance estimator. The weight of each data point is estimated using the direct estimator, and the importance approximator is updated online at test time. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on two synthetic tasks and the MuJoCo robot manipulation benchmark, where it is found to outperform the importance estimator and an existing direct estimator method on the benchmark tasks.

The development of a simulation tool has enabled researchers to investigate the optimal design of CMOS sensors by modeling the impact of material properties and geometry on sensor performance. By utilizing a Monte Carlo method, this code simulates electron impact ionization and the resulting drift of electrons and holes within the sensor's active region. The results reveal that CMOS sensors utilizing high-resistivity Czochralski substrate material exhibit superior performance compared to those with epitaxial materials, primarily due to the latter's lower intrinsic doping level and thicker depletion layer. Furthermore, the simulation indicates that increased reverse bias voltage and thinner depletion layers in epitaxial sensors can enhance their performance to match that of sensor with high-resistivity substrate.

Future space telescopes will be capable of discovering planets directly, using advanced ground-based instruments that can now image exoplanets despite challenging technical hurdles. A new method is proposed to effectively utilize the potential of the upcoming large telescopes by using advanced imaging techniques and advanced data analysis to distinguish planets from the background noise.

This study presents a novel Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, combining the effects of
two distinct C-I-R processes to mimic the impact of market friction on interest rates.
We develop a closed-form solution for the probability distribution and create
computational methods to calculate option prices. Furthermore, our model can be
readily modified to incorporate a drift term reflecting positive economic growth.

Researchers have been actively searching for sterile neutrinos, which could potentially resolve anomalies observed in neutrino oscillation experiments, such as the LSND and MiniBoone anomalies, as well as the loss of electron neutrino flux and excess of electrons in the KEK to Kamioka (K2K) experiment. In order to investigate the sterile neutrino hypothesis, the SUPER-KAMIOKANDE experiment analyzed supernova neutrino data in light of the recent sterile neutrino anomalies. By considering the sterile neutrino parameters that fit the anomalies, SUPER-KAMIOKANDE found that sterile neutrinos might produce significant effects on supernova neutrino spectra and lepton fractions. These effects include a suppression of high-energy neutrino emissions and an enhancement of low-energy neutrino emissions, which would need to be taken into account in modeling supernova neutrino spectra.

In meta-analyses involving multi-arm trials with at least 10 studies, statistical inference often relies on cluster-robust variance-covariance estimators provided by software like Stata, R, and SAS. However, these estimators are known to be inaccurate with small sample sizes, a limitation that particularly affects meta-analyses involving a small number of studies. To address this issue, we propose an alternative approach based on the mid-p correction method to improve the accuracy of cluster-robust inference in such scenarios. Our approach involves adjusting trial-level variances and using numerical methods to solve resulting equations for better effect size estimation. To handle complex situations, such as when trials overlap or arms share the same control, we employ the Tarone modification of Pearson's $\chi^2$ distribution. Our method is further enhanced by incorporating the Knapp-Hartung adjustment and the use of numerical integration to estimate the p-value. To validate our approach, we conducted simulation studies that demonstrate its accuracy in computing mid-p values and effect sizes. Our results are set to form the basis of a new implementation in the 'meta' R package.

The influence of temporal discretization on particle-fluid interactions within the PIC-DEM-FPI model is examined through simulations of particle sedimentation in turbulent flow. A novel technique to extend collision duration in the simulation is implemented, alongside two distinct methods to represent turbulent fluctuations: direct modeling and homogenization into modified fluid properties. The results indicate that extending collision duration significantly impacts simulation outcomes, particularly when using the former turbulence modeling approach. Furthermore, analyzing the phase lag between turbulent fluctuations and particle collisions reveals distinct behaviors that correlate with numerical parameters. These findings are also discussed in the context of a theoretical framework for predicting turbulence-sediment interaction.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has led researchers to examine the stress-energy tensor's stress component at the horizon of a black hole. Examine how its behavior near the horizon compares to that of a free-falling observer. On a background of a black hole formed by the collapse of matter, the stress component near the horizon has become extremely high, prompting the question of whether this energy source can sustain itself over time. Show that in such a scenario, the stress component gradually decreases and ultimately becomes negligible. As a result, the emission of radiation energy slows and eventually ceases, suggesting that in order to maintain steady-state black hole evaporation, the horizon must maintain specific characteristics. As a consequence, the notion of hovering observers extracting energy through work may not be tenable.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening in particles after passing through a nucleus is investigated using the DGLV radiation formalism. This research focuses on how broadening is related to energy radiated by fast particles and examines its implications for measuring particles' path length in substances like iron or deuterium-helium gas.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The dynamics of a liquid jet interacting with an identical stream were studied through high-speed imaging and support from computational fluid dynamics. This investigation focused on how the sheath of surrounding air formed around the jet influenced its behavior. As the air sheath collapsed and caused irregular fluctuations in the jet's cross-section, the stream began to break apart into distinct segments. This phenomenon was observed to occur at varying degrees of air sheath impingement, with the resulting droplets experiencing different levels of interaction with the surrounding fluid. Notably, as the sheath radius decreased, the size of the droplets increased, and the distribution of sizes became increasingly broad. This research provides a detailed understanding of how different factors affect the behavior of a liquid jet in its interaction with another stream of the same fluid.

In the realm of High-Performance Computing, the occurrence of hardware failures is a common occurrence, necessitating the implementation of robust error correction mechanisms. As hardware components become increasingly prone to errors, the adoption of non-volatile memories has become a critical factor in achieving fault tolerance. This paper presents an in-depth evaluation of the performance implications of integrating non-volatile memories into the memory hierarchy of Cluster-based systems, considering the costs associated with Checkpoint/Restart mechanisms versus the benefits derived from avoiding system restarts in the event of hardware failures.

Organizational frameworks, such as information hierarchies and knowledge graphs, are essential for managing complex information and making knowledge accessible.  Researchers recently explored the relationship between these two concepts and developed a novel mathematical model that defines knowledge graphs as generalized hierarchies with particular properties.  This paper delves into the analysis of this model and investigates how it can be used to create organizational structures from knowledge graphs and vice versa.  It also discusses the challenges and potential applications of this work in the context of information organization and data management.

We conducted a numerical study of non-hierarchical three-body systems consisting of two massive bodies and one massless body over extended periods of time. Our analysis focused on three distinct configurations: one involving two massive bodies orbiting each other with the third body orbiting them, one where the system consists of two bodies of equal mass orbiting a third, and a third with the same mass distribution but with the outer body having a significantly larger orbit. Our results indicate that the escape probability of the system is influenced by the initial eccentricities of the orbits and the mass distribution, but that the long-term stability of the system is not affected by these factors.

To investigate the suppression of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons, we've analyzed ALICE data from Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, specifically the experiments from 2015 and 2018. Our analysis involved normalizing the lead-lead data to proton-proton data obtained in 2015 and 2018. We've also calculated nuclear modification factors for these mesons across different energy Pb-Pb collisions, in addition to comparing their production ratios. Our findings revealed an enhancement of the relative yield of J/$\psi$ to $\psi$(2S) mesons in 2018 compared to 2015, suggesting a reduced suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons or a greater suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons in 2018.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning function forms a hyperdoctrine, and we explore the
hyperdoctrine structure in detail.

When developing software, unexpected changes can sometimes cause previously working features to malfunction. To ensure these changes don't break existing functionality, regression testing is used. This involves running a set of test cases aimed at verifying the functionality and detecting any new errors. Due to the time it takes for the testing process, especially in large projects, keeping the test suite up to date with new developments can be challenging. A method called prioritization is employed to reorder the test suite, allowing prioritized testing of the updated code and prioritized regression testing of the remaining test cases. This paper presents an innovative approach to prioritization, utilizing static analysis and code complexity metrics to automatically generate a test suite priority without the need for dynamic analysis. The method employs a graph-based approach to measure complexity between modules and uses this information to determine the priority of test cases, effectively addressing the test suite prioritization and regression testing challenges.

A 2021 study revealed that machine learning models using Electronic Health Records can accurately identify suicidal ideation, yet the models may be limited by their focus on clinical data. This research aims to address this issue by examining whether incorporating ecologically sensitive data from patients through Ecological Momentary Assessment can improve the ability of models to detect suicidal ideation. The investigation involves comparing the performance of models trained on Electronic Health Records alone to those that also include real-time data from patients, and the results show that combining these data sources yields more accurate and generalizable results, with improved AUC-ROC scores when tested on real patient information.

Our research involves a comprehensive X-ray study of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, combining observations from the 0.3-2.4 keV energy range, specifically from Chandra and XMM-Newton. This range fills a gap in previous studies, and our analysis shows that polarized X-ray emission is strongest in regions of high synchrotron activity. Our findings indicate an overall average polarization of 1.3% in this area, and our three-dimensional magnetic field reconstruction reveals a field strength of approximately 50 microGauss. Our research also provides a detailed map of the magnetic field's orientation and strength, revealing a strength of about 70 microGauss within a specific region. Furthermore, our analysis shows that polarized thermal X-ray emission is present in specific areas, and our spectral mapping reveals that this emission is strongest in specific regions, and that this emission is consistent with a specific temperature, and that this temperature is consistent with a specific age, and that this age is consistent with the age of the remnant.

Consider a set $A$ consisting of the first $n$ positive integers, with all possible subsets having sizes ranging from $1$ to $k$. Under these conditions, four distinct Brualdi conjectures concerning the integers within $[x_1, x_2]$ are explored. Specifically, a Brualdi conjecture states that a set of $k$ distinct integers can be chosen from an infinite sequence, ensuring that all subset sums fall within a specified range of integers, with similar but varied conclusions drawn in three other conjectures. These concepts are supported by related mathematical theorems and proven through a combination of existing evidence and new, yet-to-be-discovered proofs.

The characteristics of dense matter within the range of 0.5 to 5 times the nuclear saturation density are of significant interest due to its potential to inform our understanding of dense matter through observable phenomena. The speed of sound in dense matter is expected to increase with density under normal circumstances. However, at extremely high densities, the concept of massless and massful particles converges, and the speed of sound may approach that of light. Our research focuses on determining the speed of sound in dense matter at both low and high densities. We consider dense matter within the context of hydrostatic equilibrium, where the pressure and density are influenced by factors such as temperature, composition, and pressure. Our study reveals that the speed of sound behaves similarly to a damped oscillator at both low and high densities. We also find that the speed of sound can be approximated using simple mathematical expressions over a wide range of densities. Our research indicates that the difference between the measured speed of sound and that of an incompressible fluid is approximately 0.14 times the speed of light.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states created from optical resonators for use in parameter estimation with increased sensitivity. The considered states include a range of modified versions of Fock states, each resulting from different combinations of squeezing and displacement applied to the vacuum in optical cavities. The optimal state for minimum error in estimating a parameter is identified through the use of the quantum Fisher information. The relevant information is calculated for both the Fock state and the squeezed state within an optical cavity, allowing for the comparison of these primary non-classical states. The study also examines the error introduced by technical noise and demonstrates that the sensitivity achieved using the modified non-classical states can be improved over the standard squeezed state approach.

We've developed a new technique for identifying and tracking the boundaries between gas and liquid phases in videos of flowing liquids with multiple disconnected pockets.
This method employs a process called skeletonization to trace the perimeter of each isolated liquid area and has been successfully applied to analyze videos of a two-phase flow in a channel with a complex zigzag pattern created by a series of obstacles.
Our skeletonization method produced precise results and matched manual annotations closely, and has been used to calculate average film thickness and film frequency at various locations within the channel.
These data were then compared with theoretical models and experimental models developed using a group of students, and our results showed close agreement with the advanced students' data.
Overall, this skeletonization method provides a reliable and efficient tool for analyzing complex multi-pocketed liquid flows.

Researchers have developed a new physical model to examine how influenza viruses interact with surfaces that have a layer of carbohydrates. This model considers the collective movement of viral proteins and their adhesion properties, which are influenced by a range of binding strengths. It is observed that, in low temperatures, certain influenza strains exhibit similar behavior to "cold filters," which tend to cluster together on these surfaces, whereas at higher temperatures, they adopt a more random distribution pattern.

We have conducted a comprehensive study on the optical to near-infrared properties of 122 galaxies with irregularly warped disks. These galaxies were initially identified through the SDSS survey and are part of the 'Warped Galaxies' catalog. We analyzed their optical colors, sizes, and morphological features, and calculated their star formation rates using near-infrared luminosity. We compared their characteristics to a control group of galaxies with normal disks, and also examined the relationship between their warp amplitude and other physical properties. Our results show that U-shaped galaxies tend to be bluer and have higher star formation rates than S-shaped galaxies, and their sizes, colors, and star formation rates are more similar to edge-on spiral galaxies than to highly inclined elliptical galaxies. We found that the relationship between size and star formation rate is steeper for S-type galaxies compared to U-type galaxies, and that the distribution of their sizes is skewed towards smaller sizes. We found that the relationship between warp amplitude and size is complex, and that the relationship between warp amplitude and star formation rate is not straightforward. We found that the distribution of near-infrared luminosity is skewed towards lower luminosity, and that the distribution of star formation rate is skewed towards lower SFR.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Researchers have recently discovered that sound waves can be polarized in specific directions, a phenomenon known as chiral phonons. In materials with space group symmetry, the movement of atoms in a crystal structure gives rise to chiral behaviors, which can be described using a scalar product of position and velocity vectors. In the study presented here, we observed that in a material with a specific structural arrangement, the movement of atoms results in the generation of chiral phonons with significant magnitudes, which can be directly observed in Raman spectra and electron energy loss spectra. The material's properties also allow for the conversion of ordinary sound waves into surface electromagnetic waves through a process involving the coupling of electromagnetic fields with the material's chiral properties, a process that can be manipulated by adjusting external conditions. The ability to do so opens up new possibilities for the development of highly sensitive sensors and other related technologies.

In insulators, Born effective charges connect atomic displacement to polar phonons and indicate how charges respond to external fields, which is crucial for piezoelectricity and polarizability calculations. Despite its significance, calculating these charges through first-principles simulations can be computationally costly. A faster approach involves using ab-initio machine-learned interatomic potentials to calculate Born effective charges at a more reasonable computational cost. A more theoretical connection can be made between BZ-integrated and BZ-averaged Born effective charges through a connection through financial market theory.

Incompressible fluids exhibit thermal fluctuations that are negligible at lengths exceeding the Kolmogorov scale, whereas at smaller scales, they can be modeled as an incompressible fluid with thermal effects. This leads to a new class of turbulence, known as "thermal turbulence," which differs from traditional turbulence in its thermal and viscous components interacting on equal footing. Thermal turbulence exhibits thermal fluctuations at all scales, even the largest, and, at small scales, the thermal and viscous components can be balanced, leading to a new length scale, the P\'{e}clet length. We present numerical simulations of thermal turbulence and demonstrate its thermal effects, including the thermal contribution to the energy cascade and energy dissipation rate, and its impact on the energy spectrum and energy flux.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant under time-reversal symmetry. However, breaking this symmetry in the bulk also eliminates the invariant and topological protection of surface states. Our study focuses on how introducing magnetic impurities affects 3D Topological Insulators, specifically how they affect the surface conductivity. We found that magnetic impurities on the surface act as a form of "Surface Topological Protection," even when time-reversal symmetry is broken. This means that the surface conductivity remains quantized at half the quantum of conductance, $h/2e^2$, despite the presence of magnetic impurities.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, a specific type of dynamic behavior known as delayed Hopf bifurcation arises, resulting in rich patterns of oscillation. We've discovered a new way to exploit this phenomenon through time-lag modulation, revealing that it can be triggered by regular adjustments and manifest as either irregular or regular outcomes depending on the degree of Strebel number nonlinearity. Furthermore, our research shows that its period can be directly influenced by the rate of modulation, offering the opportunity to control this type of behavior for the purpose of generating reliable, modulated signals in laser technology.

We develop an operational meaning for a set of state-altering expressions in state-altering strong semantics (SASS), in a higher-order setting. Our adequacy theorem confirms that the computed results match expected outcomes. The criteria for SASS are quite strict: it must track memory usage, account for variable changes, and account for an infinite memory capacity. Consequently, traditional methods for higher-order state-management, like Box-Router and Permutation models, are incompatible with the required criteria for our adequacy theorem. Our solution involves reformulating strict semantics as a specific type of process interaction, using a modified version of Berry and Curien's interaction process model. Our strict semantics is derived from an operational definition using a type of expression similar to that in Reynolds's model of permutation models. The key innovation is using a type of expression that can refer to itself, combined with a type-theoretic approach to modeling higher-order state, specifically using a variation of the do-calculus introduced by Birtwistle and Morrisett.

Discussions between programmers about design decisions during development are a key aspect of creating software systems.  In the field of data science, analyzing these discussions is a common task.  However, there is a lack of unified standards for defining these discussions in the industry.  To address this, researchers are interested in exploring how to automatically identify discussions on design decisions within the interface of collaborative platforms.  This paper presents a novel approach for defining and detecting these discussions based on predefined topics within structured interfaces, specifically within the context of GitHub Issues.  The study presents a dataset containing  GitHub Issues related to predefined topics and shows that design mining can be effectively applied to detect these discussions on issues.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter. Dark energy is represented as a form of vacuum energy resulting from an infinite number of harmonic oscillators, each with its own energy level, related to the density of dark energy. These oscillators, referred to as zero-point fluctuations, generate the vacuum energy, which in turn produces the cosmological constant, responsible for dark energy. In addition, the model suggests that the momentum of these oscillators is the source of dark matter, which exerts a repulsive force on massive particles, effectively representing gravity. As a result, the model not only accounts for dark energy, which drives the accelerated expansion of the universe, but also explains dark matter, which has a repulsive effect on matter, opposing gravitational attraction.

Proximal methods, which employ an iterative process, are commonly used to solve
optimization problems that are smooth or have specific nonsmooth properties.
This paper compares two variants of the proximal gradient method for nonsmooth
optimization problems and proposes two formulas for the step size parameter.
We demonstrate the validity of these formulas using two examples and show that
they perform similarly, providing a framework for using one variant in the other
and providing a reference for implementing the more complex variant.

We introduce a new concept of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in commutative rings with a multiplicative identity, and proceed to examine its fundamental properties. Additionally, we investigate how this notion relates to other types of prime ideals, and establish connections between various weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying to $ho^-$ and $
u_	au$, and $B^+$ decaying to $ho^0$ and $
u_	au$. By combining multiple statistical analyses, the total probability of these decays has been determined. For $B^0$ decaying to $ho^-$ and $
u_	au$, the total probability of decay is found to be $3.16$ with an associated uncertainty of $0.64$ and $0.34$, respectively. For $B^+$ decaying to $ho^0$ and $
u_	au$, the total probability of decay is found to be $3.14$ with an associated uncertainty of $0.63$ and $0.32$, respectively. These measurements are significant as they represent the first instances where such decay processes were observed and the most precise to date. Furthermore, when compared to theoretical predictions, the results for $B^0$ decaying to $ho^-$ and $
u_	au$, and $B^+$ decaying to $ho^0$ and $
u_	au$, are consistent with the predictions, although the predictions carry a significant margin of error.

A cutting-edge technique called photonic spectroscopy is rapidly gaining attention due to its ability to provide an affordable and compact alternative to traditional methods. By utilizing customized spectral responses from compact photonic devices, this innovative approach enables researchers to gather meaningful data about various substances. In this groundbreaking study, researchers successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of photonic spectroscopy by training and validating sophisticated machine learning models capable of accurately classifying different types of strawberries based on their internal quality. To achieve this, researchers combined data from photonic spectroscopy with high-resolution imaging techniques and used various advanced classification methods to provide detailed internal quality assessments. This ground-breaking work validates the potential for photonic spectroscopy to provide precise and reliable assessments of food quality in real-time, thereby paving the way for its application in diverse settings.

In the last few years, machine learning models have aimed to predict various issues such as polypharmacy, medication interactions, and unnecessary prescriptions. However, these models often lack transparency in their decision-making process, which can be a concern in medical settings where the implications of their predictions are significant. To address this, we propose a new model called MultiMed, which aims to improve upon existing models by providing more accurate and comprehensive predictions about a patient's medication regimen. To evaluate the performance of our model, we developed a new dataset consisting of real patient data and annotated with relevant information.

Several local governments face difficulties in deploying advanced technologies for
evaluating road damage due to several factors, such as high initial costs and
complexity in maintenance. A potential solution involves utilizing open-source
software and dataset. Our research focuses on a modular, customizable platform
for collecting, processing, and visualizing data, which can be easily adapted
by various users. This includes developing a comprehensive roadmap for collecting
road damage evidence using a specific, freely available dataset and equipment.

Imitation learning has gained prominence as a viable approach in various domains, allowing agents to learn from expert demonstrations rather than requiring the meticulous design of reward functions. This method's primary benefit lies in its ability to quickly train and deploy agents. Nonetheless, imitation learning often results in policies that merely replicate external behavior, limiting their adaptability to novel situations. In contrast, process-value learning seeks to internalize and understand the underlying process, aiming to develop more resilient policies. This research integrates process-value learning with imitation learning, enabling the creation of self-sustaining policies by framing it as a series of dynamic programming problems. By incorporating process learning into demonstration-based learning, our framework surpasses existing methods in its ability to generalize and adapt to unforeseen circumstances.

A significant factor in the formation of early galaxies and stars is the amplification of magnetic fields. To investigate its impact on star formation, computer simulations were conducted in 3D to model the motion of magnetic fields within a rotating layer of gas. As the simulation progressed, small fluctuations in density were amplified, leading to the development of spiral patterns. The magnetic field's tension caused these features to become more defined, ultimately resulting in the development of distinct, star-forming regions. The magnetic field's strength was significantly amplified, reaching up to 10 microgauss, and the density reached up to 10^-19 g cm^-3. The simulation showed the formation of secondary protostars, with densities as high as 10^-17 g cm^-3, and the magnetic field was amplified by a factor of 1000. The findings suggest that the magnetic field's role in the universe is more significant than previously thought, and the simulation provides a framework for further research into the impact of magnetic fields on star formation.

Mining association rules within datasets is a fundamental concept in data analysis.
Each rule within the set has associated confidence and support metrics, influencing its significance.
Higher confidence and support values indicate stronger associations between items, whereas lower values indicate weaker associations.
Lower confidence values can result in spurious associations, necessitating methods to identify such cases.
This paper presents a method for detecting spurious association rules by leveraging a Bayesian approach, incorporating prior information about the relationship between variables.
The method employs a Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the posterior probability of variable independence, providing a measure of confidence for each rule.
Spurious rules are identified based on the estimated probability threshold, providing a more accurate assessment of rule validity.

Individuals within the criminal justice system often suffer from mental health issues, which, if untreated, can cause them to re-offend. In a study, the effectiveness of mental health treatment during the probation period was evaluated in terms of its impact on the likelihood of offenders returning to the criminal justice system. Utilizing data from South Carolina, the research employed instrumental variable regression analysis to assess how access to treatment influenced recidivism rates. It was discovered that mental health treatment during probation reduces the likelihood of offenders re-offending in both count and binary forms, contradicting previous research that suggested treatment had no significant effect.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are crucial for situational awareness, enabling wireless systems to
make informed decisions. These maps provide a detailed understanding of the radio
environment, assisting various wireless communications, including UAVs, in
overcoming obstacles and identifying optimal positions. However, traditional
safety systems for aviation, which rely on ground-based equipment, are largely
unaware of the radio environment, limiting their ability to ensure safe UAV
navigation. This study presents an approach to building accurate radio maps using
UAVs and ground-based sensors, leveraging their advanced navigation capabilities
to collect essential data. This data is then utilized to create a reliable model
of the surrounding area, empowering smart UAVs to access critical information
and make data-driven decisions.

This research focuses on developing a framework for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series data by combining multiple detection methods. We combine Hidden Markov Models and Page's test to create a system that flags potential issues and then uses a contrasting algorithm to confirm them. To minimize false alarms, we set a dynamic threshold for the confirmation step based on the initial detection. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through simulations of discrete time series data and compared to individual and other ensemble-based methods. We find that our method outperforms these alternatives in terms of reducing false alarms and accurately capturing the timing and duration of unusual patterns.

This study presents and evaluates a novel verification system that integrates audio, visual, and behavioral modalities for more reliable person identification. We also introduce a comprehensive dataset consisting of video clips featuring strangers performing various authentication tasks, which we utilize to compare a neural network-based behavioral feature extraction method with traditional approaches. Our findings demonstrate that the trimodal system yields superior accuracy in verification and is robust against verification errors stemming from variations in task execution. Notably, the dataset reveals that combining auditory, visual, and behavioral data results in accurate verification even in the presence of potential spoofing attempts, which our method effectively detects and prevents.

This study examines the effectiveness of additional training using enhanced data on speech models. We focus on enhancing Transformer and Conformer models with synthetic distortions derived from LogMel spectrograms and real-world distortions from speech samples. Our analysis reveals that using augmented data significantly improves the performance of pre-trained models, with synthetic distortions providing a substantial 3.3% relative improvement over baseline models without additional training. Notably, real-world distortions from speech samples also yield a notable 2.1% relative improvement. Moreover, our findings indicate that combining both distortions results in the best outcome, with notable gains observed in notable speech recognition models such as Whisper large and VoxPopuli.

In many statistical applications, researchers are interested in characterizing a population through its mixing distribution, which can be viewed as the distribution of a random variable. The Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) has proven effective in estimating this distribution, but it has significant drawbacks, including sensitivity to outliers and non-existence in certain cases. To address these issues, this paper Generalizes MLE by developing Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) for mixing distributions, which GMLE can effectively estimate a mixing distribution even with outliers present. The theoretical underpinnings of GMLE are established, including the convergence of GMLE to the true mixing distribution as sample size increases, which is demonstrated through the consistency of GMLE. The proposed GMLE method is further validated through numerical experiments, which show its ability to accurately recover the mixing distribution in the presence of various types of contamination.

In the realm of in situ data analysis, a scenario arises where data is released immediately, rather than being delayed for post-hoc processing.  This type of data release is referred to as in situ data release.  A key challenge in this context is ensuring the privacy of the dataset, which is complicated by the fact that an adversary can infer information about the dataset in real-time.  To address this issue, researchers have developed One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP), a framework that allows for private data analysis in real-time.  The problem of OSDP is particularly difficult because the adversary can compute the impact of each data point on the output in real-time.  To address this issue, researchers have developed an algorithm that can provide (ε,δ)-OSDP for a Gaussian mechanism with arbitrary δ > 0.  The authors also establish a lower bound on the number of data points required to achieve this privacy goal.

The distribution of dust in protoplanetary disks is a crucial indicator of planet formation, yet disk substructures may also arise from interactions with a planet or protoplanetary drag. To investigate this phenomenon, we conducted numerical simulations of gas and dust dynamics in protoplanetary disks containing one or two planets. Our study utilized three-dimensional simulations of gas flow and particle tracking to model the disk environment, taking into account thermal balance and magnetic effects. The results indicate that disk features such as local gas density variations, temperature differences, and altered magnetic properties can significantly influence dust accumulation patterns. Consequently, observing dust accumulation alone may not be sufficient evidence for the presence of a planet.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, yet its complexity lies in the vast amount of data points coupled with diverse analytical requirements. To address this, we've developed TimeTagger, an open-source Python library designed to simplify time-stamped data analysis. Building on existing concepts, such as histograms and reduced-order modeling, TimeTagger provides an innovative approach to handling large datasets with numerous dimensions.

We establish the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constrained velocity and a nonconvex cost function, under the condition that the data is Lipschitz continuous.

Researchers have been investigating the nature of stellar structures, often referred to as strings, which were initially thought to be physical formations within the galaxy. A study examined the string-like structure known as Mayorski's Chain, analyzing its constituent stars' ages, velocities, and chemical composition. Contrary to expectations of a bound object, the analysis revealed no uniform characteristics among the stars, suggesting that this structure is more likely a coincidental alignment of dispersing stellar streams rather than a singular physical formation.

The visual appeal of fashion outfits is influenced by specific characteristics of individual garments, such as their color, pattern, and level of detail. Current methods for outfit recommendation focus on matching these aspects but are limited by their use of basic color analysis and basic feature matching. In this project, we have developed an advanced color extraction technique that accurately identifies the dominant colors in images of garments, and a more precise pattern matching method that compares the visual appearance of garments, rather than just their basic features. Our technique for determining detail similarity measures the visual complexity of garments, and we have used it to create a new approach for outfit recommendation that prioritizes visual compatibility. The efficacy of this method has been validated through extensive testing on a large dataset of women's clothing, and our results show that it significantly outperforms the traditional method of matching garment colors, details, and visual style.

In the framework of quantum resource theory, the principle of local operations and shared randomness (LOS) serves as the standard for permissible actions when dealing with systems containing extra quantum resources. This paper focuses on examining the systems resource of nonquantum states and operations, often referred to as "mixed state channels," within the framework of the standard quantum theory.
