In this research, we examine the category of local modules over the category of twisted quantum groups, specifically related to a finite subgroup of the multiplicative complex numbers. The orbifolds that are exceptional in nature fall into four categories, which can be represented as pairs of numbers: (3,1), (3,2), (5,2), and (7,2). The simple objects within these exceptional orbifides are defined, and our findings confirm the conjecture proposed by Mazorchuk and Wang, also revealing a direct relationship between certain auto-equivalences and the concept of Hall algebras.

We examine the Fisher-KPP equation in continuous space, along with an discrete approximation based on a stochastic process that involves binomial branching and spatial movement. As the approximation's grid becomes increasingly fine, with associated time scaling, we demonstrate that the difference between the approximate model and the continuous model converges at a rate of $N^{-1/3}$ in probability.

This study introduces a dataset comprising handwritten mathematical terms and their cursive versions, then proposes an innovative approach to classify modern handwritten terms. The method leverages a binary classifier to distinguish mathematical symbols from other characters, followed by recognition using Hidden Markov Models and Template Matching. The dataset, named HMT-Char, contains binary images of individual characters in four distinct styles, captured using a digital pen on a tablet. The recognition pipeline combines HMM-based clustering and template matching to achieve high accuracy, with the classifier demonstrating a remarkable success rate of 99.2%.

This research addresses duration modeling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by introducing an innovative approach to phoneme-level duration modeling. Unlike traditional methods that model the mean and dispersion of phoneme durations, our approach models the median and interquartile range. We demonstrate that considering the median as a more representative measure for typical durations is more beneficial than the mean. Furthermore, we show that the regression-based method is sufficient for this purpose. To achieve this, we develop a novel feature set that effectively captures the necessary acoustic information. All components of our method are designed to be fully compatible with other phoneme-level phonetic features.

Species distribution assessment is a crucial task in ecology, and understanding
the locations of individual species is essential for effective environmental
conservation efforts. Several statistical models have been developed to estimate
species distribution based on observations that may be inaccurate. We examined
the estimation accuracy of the Single Template method in relation to species size,
ecosystem complexity, and the presence of multiple species, and compared it to
other popular ecologically-based approaches, including the Popular, Ecologically
Based, and Neighbourhood Matching methods. Our findings demonstrate that the
Simple Template method outperforms its counterparts, particularly in environments
with smaller species and higher levels of complexity.

A new method combining deep learning and interactive techniques has been developed to enhance the accuracy of diagnosing malignant skin cancer from dermatoscopic images. This approach leverages the strengths of both expert dermatologists and深度学习 models to improve diagnostic performance. A comparative study was conducted on a large dataset of dermatoscopic images, comparing the performance of the new method to that of experienced dermatologists. This approach showed significant improvements over the dermatologists in specific cases, with notable diagnostic precision gains of 9.6% in certain exams. A system demonstration is available online at http://www.derminteractive.com/.

This study presents a probabilistic autoencoder method that utilizes Type Ia supernovae spectral information to create reduced data representations. By applying the technique, we discovered that it can identify a set of underlying spectral patterns and corresponding coefficients from the data. When these patterns are analyzed, we discovered that the resulting principal components resemble known spectral features and coefficients, and that the associated wavelengths span the range of 4000-9000 Angstroms. Furthermore, we discovered that these components are linked to variations in SN Ia properties, such as their luminosity and light curve shapes, and that these associations are consistent with previous studies. In addition, we found that using a probabilistic approach allowed us to quantify the uncertainty in our reduced data set, and that this uncertainty is influenced by factors such as the number of data points and signal-to-noise ratio, and that this uncertainty is correlated with photometric errors, and that this finding is significant for future studies that use this reduced data set.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been detected in a dusty galaxy using ALMA, and its characteristics were analyzed in detail. Our research reveals that the outflow's gas mass is approximately $1.2 \times 10^{9}$ solar masses, and its mass rate is approximately $0.4 \times 10^{9}$ solar masses per year. Our data suggest that the outflow has an extended velocity structure, and its morphology appears to be complex and multi-directional. Our analysis indicates that the outflow may have multiple origins, and its morphology could be the result of a combination of a galaxy disk and a conical outflow. Our research reveals that the outflow has a gas mass that exceeds the galaxy's total gas mass, and its volume density is approximately $0.03$ solar masses per cubic parsec. Our data suggest that the outflow is not gravitationally unstable, and its dynamics could be explained by a combination of a galaxy disk and a conical outflow. Our research reveals that the outflow has a low metallicity, and its properties are similar to those of a "super-wind" observed in another galaxy. Our data suggest that the outflow is not sufficient to quench star formation in the galaxy, and its properties are consistent with a "super-wind" that is observed in a galaxy at a redshift of 2.1.

To investigate the impact of particle density on turbulent plume dynamics,
experiments were conducted in a tank with continuous inflow of fluid and heavier
or lighter streams, creating a distinct axisymmetric plume. By utilizing PIV
velocity measurements and DPM analysis, we calculated relevant flow parameters
and found that the plume's growth rate is influenced by the direction of
entrance fluxes, regardless of particle density. Furthermore, we observed that
particle distribution within the plume is not uniform, showing variations along
its axis, and that this variance increases with density ratio.

Understanding the spread of epidemics within complex networks is crucial for developing effective containment strategies. Traditional approaches that model disease propagation using contact graphs have been informative, but they fall short in capturing the full context of host interactions. In reality, diseases often spread through face-to-face encounters that are influenced by various social and environmental factors, which can be more accurately represented by grouping contacts into clusters. We've developed a hypergraph-based model that incorporates these factors as hyperedges representing groups of individuals interacting simultaneously. By combining this model with the Smallworld property, we've been able to simulate the spread of diseases in various scenarios and identify the most effective nodes for implementing vaccination or testing interventions.

Recently, researchers have made significant progress in studying 2D magnetic semiconductors, particularly in CrI$_3$, which exhibits magnetic properties that change based on its thickness. Studies have shown that canting of the magnetic spins can have a significant impact on the material's response to light. To better understand this phenomenon, we developed a comprehensive theory that takes into account the complex structure of CrI$_3$ and discovered that light can induce the magnetic spins to precess in a specific way. Our findings also reveal that light can induce the magnetic spins to precess in a specific way, opening the door to controlling the material's properties using light.

We've developed a model to analyze the behavior of the magnetorotational instability in solar-type stars, incorporating effects from the Rossby number, magnetic field geometry, and differential rotation speed. The model reveals that the interaction between the magnetic field and differential rotation is influenced by the Rossby number, and the transition from geostrophic to non-geostrophic dynamics is gradual, and can occur at Ro values greater than 0.1. We've found that the behavior of the magnetorotational instability is largely unaffected by the magnetic field's orientation, and the transition from axisymmetric to non-axisymmetric modes is gradual, and can happen at high Ro values. The model also shows that the growth rate of the magnetorotational instability is maximized when the radial component of the magnetic field is present, and the dependence of the growth rate on the winding mode is consistent with previous findings. We've found that the behavior of the magnetorotational instability is similar in solar-type stars and accretion disks, and the model can be applied to accretion disks with a geometrically thin and optically thick structure.

A new K-fan deep model architecture is introduced to process multiple input sources simultaneously, offering a compact and efficient alternative for combining information from different modalities without necessitating a large number of parameters. The model's summing layers enable smooth learning and facilitate the integration of multiple input modes. The benefits of this structure were tested in multiple scenarios, including multiple object image recognition, multiple object identification, character classification, emotion analysis, and multiple class identification. The results demonstrate that the model achieves comparable accuracy to traditional models with fewer parameters. Additionally, theoretical analysis supports the benefits of this structure, providing a solid foundation for its development.

The challenge of verifying multi-threaded programs lies in the fact that existing testing methods, such as unit and functional testing, cannot effectively detect infrequent race conditions. To address this issue, we've developed an automated approach that uses coverage-guided mutation testing to detect race conditions, which has been found to be more effective than traditional testing methods. Our solution involves integrating race condition detection into coverage and mutation frameworks, and we've demonstrated its efficacy through experiments on several real-world programs, yielding positive results.

The ability to share messages on WhatsApp enables rapid dissemination of information, but also facilitates the spread of misinformation. Although existing research has explored the spread of fake news on Twitter, the impact of misinforming on private messaging platforms like WhatsApp remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we aim to address this gap by examining the impact of misinforming messages on private messaging, specifically WhatsApp. We model the private dissemination of misinformation as a function of the probability of forwarding messages and the likelihood of spreading false information, which is influenced by public exposure to misinforming messages. We then compare the predicted outcomes of our model with the observed behavior of actual WhatsApp users, and find that the model accurately predicts the spread of misinformation in real WhatsApp groups.

We examine the frequency spectrum in a branching population where individuals have a finite set of types. Types evolve over time through mutation and the population reproduces via a mechanism that can be either random or fully determined. When the population size is large, our analysis focuses on how the frequency spectrum changes and the conditions under which it converges to a stable state. Our findings indicate that both a sufficiently high probability of mutation and a large population size are necessary for convergence in the discrete-time model. Conversely, in the continuous-time model, only a large population size is required for convergence. Our analysis also reveals a new stochastic process representing the frequency spectrum in both models and the establishment of a functional limit theorem for both scenarios.

To enhance the spoofing countermeasure system's accuracy and robustness, we've developed a novel neural network module, the Attention Rectified Linear Unit (AReLU). This module incorporates two key characteristics, parameter sparsity and structured weights, to optimize model interpretability without compromising its performance. The AReLU module's parameter sparsity is achieved through a shared, binary mask that's pruned using the Extremal Optimization algorithm. Additionally, the AReLU module employs structured weights, dividing a weight vector into sub-vectors, each allocated to specific input features, to allocate computational resources efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that pruned AReLU-based models outperform both heavily unpruned AReLU and minimally pruned DenseUnits models on the PolyPhonK dataset in spoofing detection and classification tasks.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model, is a prime candidate for describing particle physics beyond the current model. However, the plan to integrate supersymmetry into the model through supergravity poses challenges in developing inflationary models due to issues with moduli fields, which require stabilization to avoid dominating the dynamics. We explore in detail the problems associated with moduli fields and their impact on cosmology, focusing on scalar field dynamics, potential barriers, and the generation of unwanted particles during reheating. We then investigate potential solutions, including the use of symmetries to create protected inflationary models, the role of heavy mediators in non-supersymmetrical reheating, and the potential for producing significant amounts of dark matter through the scattering of scalar particles.

Nonreciprocal optical systems exhibit distinct correlations of photon pairs when measured in opposed directions of propagation. We demonstrate this phenomenon through experiments conducted in two setups: disjoint ring cavities and linear cavities with two coupled modes. These demonstrations occur without requiring prior knowledge of direction, and ring and linear cavities show consistent results. The findings are consistent with classical theory and do not require the inherent nonreciprocity of radiation pressure to be valid. The verified phenomenon serves as a reliable indicator of nonreciprocity and has the potential to be used as a practical tool for detecting and characterizing optical isolators and circulators.

Superconducting quantum circuits face material flaws that generate noisy noise sources, compromising the accuracy of quantum computations. To address this issue, researchers have developed error correction techniques, yet these solutions increase the complexity of the correction process. In this study, we present an innovative approach to actively correct errors in real-time, utilizing a novel method to monitor and adjust noisy components without needing to know their specific characteristics in advance.

In 1919, Hausdorff made significant contributions to set theory by identifying specific conditions under which the real line can be divided into specific types of subsets of the real numbers. Specifically, he demonstrated that the real line can be segmented into subsets that are either countable, have uncountable cardinalities of $\aleph_1$, or have uncountable cardinalities of $\aleph_2$. However, his work also led to a notable consequence: the failure of the principle known as Martin's Axiom in certain circumstances. Subsequently, Tarski in 1930 showed that the principle of Martin's Axiom implies the nonexistence of one of these specific types of subsets when the cardinality is $\aleph_1$. More recently, Foreman and Magidor in 1995 found an interesting duality in the field, discovering that the principle of Martin's Axiom combined with the existence of a specific large cardinal, denoted as $\kappa$, leads to the existence of a particular type of subset in the real numbers that causes the failure of the principle in question.

Our analysis of historical data from commodity trading advisors reveals varying levels of predictive capability for their strategies. Notably, many CTA strategies failed to outperform a basic benchmark in more recent years, possibly due to the negative impact of traders who rely on short-term reversal strategies, which can significantly hinder CTAs' ability to generate profits. However, CTA strategies that employ fundamental analysis methods have demonstrated resilience and continued success. These findings have important implications for the investment industry and the evaluation of CTA strategies.

Identifying the application layer protocol is a crucial step in network security monitoring and intrusion detection. However, accurately determining the protocol can be challenging due to obfuscation techniques used by attackers to evade detection and obscure malicious activities. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that combines rule-based classification with machine learning to improve accuracy. By using domain-specific rules to identify commonly obfuscated protocols, we enhance the reliability of our protocol identification system. Through experiments on two real-world datasets containing both malicious and benign applications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in distinguishing between real and fake activities.

Electromagnetic waves are being used to transfer and store information, but they are limited by the wavelength being comparable to or larger than the size of the system, which restricts miniaturization. However, alternative information carriers called magnons, which arise from collective behavior in magnetic materials, are theoretically capable of achieving a much smaller system limit. A new approach combines photonic and phononic elements to create hybrid light-sound systems that can be scaled down to the nanometer level. In this work, we demonstrate the integration of these two concepts using a nanomagnetic structure that couples with light and sound, resulting in the formation of hybrid light-phonon-magnon states that exist within a narrow frequency range and occupy a minimal space. In addition, we found that coupling between these hybrid states can be manipulated by adjusting the angle of incidence of light, resulting in the emergence of nonreciprocal behavior, which has potential applications in isolated devices and sensors.

A significant advancement in deep learning applications has been achieved through federated learning, which balances user privacy and efficiency by avoiding the need to transfer data to a central server. This approach, however, results in models trained separately due to the unique data characteristics of individual users. This paper introduces a new method for training within individual data sets without sacrificing performance, utilizing a technique called label sharing. This approach enables communication of only labels among data sets, minimizing communication overhead and cost. The proposed method employs a dynamic label selection process that considers each data sample's contribution to the learning process. The efficiency of our approach is further enhanced through the use of an optimized data sampling algorithm that minimizes the need for labels. Experimental results demonstrate the exceptional performance of our method, which results in nearly identical test accuracy to the optimal model trained with the full data set, using only 1% labels.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to analyze high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically focusing on Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states and their high-dimensional equivalents. Our developed protocol enables the complete characterization of single particles derived from high-dimensional GHZ states via trace-distance measures. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to efficiently identify high-dimensional entangled states using a combination of resources, including high-dimensional GHZ states, its single particle states, and low-dimensional entanglement. These innovative techniques offer a more efficient and robust method for conducting high-dimensional quantum information processing and risk assessment.

This research focuses on addressing the critical challenge of uplink channel estimation in modern multi-user systems that utilize intelligent-reflecting-surface technology. A novel two-stage approach has been developed to efficiently determine the direct and reflected channel components, leveraging a specific property of the power associated with the reflected paths. In the initial stage of the process, the direct channel is estimated using a specific code under the assumption that the power associated with the reflected paths adheres to a specific upper limit. A specific optimization problem is then formulated to effectively utilize a specific portion of the allowed power, resulting in enhanced estimation performance. A specific code-optimization problem is then formulated as a specific semidefinite-optimization problem that can be solved in a computationally efficient manner. In the subsequent stage of the process, the residual error resulting from the initial estimation is exploited to refine the estimation of the reflected channel components. A specific optimization problem is formulated to effectively utilize a specific portion of the allowed power in order to optimize performance. A specific Bayesian-Cram\'er-Rao-bound expression is derived to provide a specific metric for evaluating the achievable performance. A specific set of simulations were conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed technique and demonstrate the significant performance gains it offers.

This study examines the connection between COVID-19 awareness as measured by local news articles and community infection and death rates. A dataset of over 10 million articles from 550 US newspapers between March 2020 and January 2021 was analyzed using natural language processing to extract mentions of "COVID-19," then had its articles counted and averaged by county. Comparing this to data from the US Census Bureau, we found that regional variations in COVID mentions initially tracked with mention of deaths in 2020, but later decoupled during the second half of the year. However, COVID mentions continued to align with infection rates throughout the study period. Aligning county-level data with the county seat location improved the fit between infection mentions and rates. These findings were utilized to develop predictive models for infection and death rates one week in advance that outperformed models based on the US Census Bureau's data.

Children's ability to count is typically introduced around the age of two, yet they often struggle to grasp its underlying principles until approximately three years of age. This discrepancy led us to investigate the possibility that counting might be learned gradually through a series of distinct stages, rather than as a continuous process. To test this hypothesis, we created a novel framework for analyzing children's counting abilities by examining the relationships between individual numbers. Using this framework, we investigated the development of number relationships in children's minds, focusing on three distinct types of connections: the link between consecutive numbers, the link between numbers that are two apart, and the link between numbers that are three apart. Our results, obtained from evaluating the counting abilities of 120 children between the ages of two and five, revealed the existence of an inflection point at the age of three, marking a significant shift in how children understand consecutive numbers. Moreover, the rate at which consecutive and bi-inflectional connections develop is found to be comparable. This study provides the first evidence of distinct stages in learning to count, thereby offering a foundation for further research into the underlying mechanisms of this complex cognitive process.

Bloom filters are widely used, space-efficient, constant-size data structures for set membership verification, but they can produce false positives. In contrast, the cuckoo filter, a variation of the Bloom filter, offers a space-efficient alternative with the ability to accurately determine set membership in the presence of only negative errors. This study introduces the wildcard cuckoo filter, a new data structure that further minimizes mistakes in standard cuckoo filters by allowing the use of wildcards as entries. We propose two methods for implementing the wildcard cuckoo filter, one of which involves a two-stage filtering process using a Bloom filter and a new variant of the wildcard cuckoo filter that we call the epsilon-cuckoo filter. We have developed an algorithm for optimizing the performance of this two-stage filtering process and conducted simulations to evaluate its efficiency.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored in this report. The underlying framework involves comparing convex geometry with the geometric properties of line bundles. The relationships between positive products and mixed volumes in convex geometry, as well as those between intersection numbers and line bundle properties on algebraic varieties demonstrated by Kleiner and B\'{i}r\'{o}, are particularly noteworthy examples. A central concept introduced is that of a Hermitian product between a K\"ahler metric and a holomorphic line bundle, which generalises and encompasses both cases while maintaining the key properties observed in each original comparison.

A new approach to forecasting future prices of a stock market index has been developed, focusing on how the trading volume of individual shares impacts the price of the entire index. By examining the relationship between these two factors, our price prediction model utilizes a machine learning algorithm to analyze the historical data and develop a predictive model. The predicted future prices are then used to create a time series, which is used to forecast the future direction of the price using another machine learning algorithm. The results demonstrate that our model is capable of accurately predicting short-term price movements, although it is important to note that no investment strategy based on our predictions has been developed.

This paper presents an innovative technique to safeguard federated learning against malicious attacks and data breaches. Methods such as Byzantine robust aggregation and differential privacy are combined to create a reliable and secure communication channel between the server and clients. Specifically, we integrate the Byzantine-Median and Laplace noise methods to achieve this goal. A crucial aspect of our approach involves devising an optimized method to minimize noise addition on the part of clients, which in turn leads to the development of a novel aggregation method dubbed "Federated Learning with Byzantine-Median and Selective Differential Privacy (FL-BSDP)." Experiments conducted on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets have demonstrated that our algorithm yields improved results compared to existing solutions in terms of accuracy and scalability.

A key challenge in research on autonomous vehicle operation is developing an effective method to learn optimal driving strategies through trial and error. In this study, an agent is developed to navigate environments with multiple possible paths. The goal of the agent is to reach a designated destination while avoiding obstacles and minimizing travel distance. The success of each action is evaluated based on how close it brings the agent to the destination. The study demonstrates the feasibility of using a specific algorithm to learn optimal routes in complex environments. In testing, the agent was able to successfully reach its target in 99.5% of the trials.

Significant advancements in deep learning technology have led to the rapid development of deepfake, a virtual production technique that creates highly realistic but potentially misleading content. Although deepfake has various legitimate uses such as film production and visual effects, its potential for fabricating false information and causing social harm cannot be overlooked. Its prevalence has heightened the need for an effective deepfake detection method. Although existing approaches have shown some promise, they often struggle with generalization and performance degradation when encountering adversarial examples. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework called HyperFakeDetector, which utilizes kernel methods to classify deepfake media and achieve superior performance across multiple domains without requiring domain-specific adaptation.

The discovery of K2-288b, a small exoplanet with a radius similar to that of Neptune, orbiting a star with low mass, has sparked interest in its potential to host a water-based ocean. However, its proximity to its host star raises concerns about the presence of a protective magnetic field. Our analysis of this concern involves examining the conditions necessary for magnetic activity in K2-288b. We find that if its mass is at least 0.12 times that of Neptune, it would have a significant magnetic field, making an ocean on its surface a plausible possibility. Our results also indicate that the likelihood of such a low-mass, ocean-hosting planet in the habitable zone of a star with low mass is around 0.008 times the frequency of Earth-based oceans.

We introduce a novel model of a binary neuron network that learns sequences through random input, based on an established model of synaptic connections between neurons. The new model incorporates connections that strengthen with sequence-based inputs, similar to existing models, but also develops connections that weaken as they are not part of the sequence, which are found to enhance learning. The effect of asymmetry in the model's connections, where connections can both strengthen and weaken, is found to significantly improve its functionality. The model's ability to create neurons that respond selectively to sequences in the library and maintain persistent activity, which is essential for sequence learning, is enhanced with connections that weaken as they are not part of the sequence. The model's performance is evaluated through the proportion of neurons that respond selectively to sequences and the accuracy of distinguishing between different sequences, which are both improved with connections that weaken as they are not part of the sequence.

For real-world applications, an OCR system must be capable of processing various text formats, such as text appearing on images taken from different angles or with distorted sizes, some of which may not have been encountered during training. Current OCR models typically rely on a fixed set of text samples for training, making them ineffective at recognizing new text formats. In response, we introduce SceneText-Auto, a novel data augmentation technique that leverages automatic text generation to create additional, diverse training instances. By using an existing text font model, we create new text images with different content, increasing the variety of training data and improving the accuracy of OCR models. When combined with existing OCR models and recurrent neural network recognizers, SceneText-Auto significantly outperforms previous methods on challenging datasets, achieving a 4.4% relative improvement on the IIIL dataset.

A specific type of chaos expansions can be applied to resolve differential equations with uncertain parameters or stochastic sources. These expansions approximate solutions by combining deterministic coefficients with polynomial functions that depend on random variables, where the coefficients are determined using standard methods for solving the underlying equation. This approach simplifies the solution process and allows for a more efficient handling of stochastic problems.

In industrial settings, monitoring complex, high-dimensional data streams is a pressing issue. The effectiveness of existing methods relies heavily on the availability of accurate and relevant reference data, which is often difficult to obtain due to the inherent difficulties in tracking the behavior of evolving systems over time. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel change detection method that operates in real-time on both mean and covariance variations in multi-variable data streams, without requiring a reference dataset. This method employs a combination of statistical techniques, including high-dimensional data decomposition and optimized search algorithms, to efficiently analyze incoming data and detect system changes. Our approach leverages a dynamic model of the observed system, allowing it to adapt to the ongoing data flow and provide accurate change detection results. To further optimize its performance, we developed an efficient algorithm that balances accuracy and computational efficiency. Through extensive simulations and real-world data tests, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in various scenarios, providing a reliable and adaptable solution for high-dimensional data stream monitoring.

The analysis of specific stellar orbits within the Milky Way's outer halo has enabled researchers to estimate when two dwarf galaxies, Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1, initially merged with the galaxy. By applying a simple model, it has been possible to determine that these two entities fell into the Milky Way approximately 4.5 billion and 9.5 billion years ago, respectively, in good agreement with previous findings. This model's accuracy has been validated through its application to the movement of stars within the globular cluster NGC 1853, resulting in a derived age that closely matches the age of this cluster.

For a profinite group G and an appropriate G[[G]]-module M, we develop an homotopy orbit spectral sequence that converges to the continuous homology H_n(G,M). In instances where M meets specific finiteness criteria, this spectral sequence gives rise to a finite-convergent approximation of H_n(G,M). In cases where M is particularly adaptable, this approximation can be expressed in terms of profinite group cohomology.

The visual complexity of documents such as invoices poses a significant challenge in creating models that can automatically extract key information. While existing methods typically focus on identifying specific regions within a document, there is less emphasis on establishing connections between these regions. To address this gap, we propose a new approach that combines existing techniques with a new type of attention mechanism. This model, which we call the structured semantic attention network, incorporates a region-specific attention mechanism that enables regions to interact with one another in a more organized and hierarchical manner. When tested on the INR2Text dataset, our approach outperformed existing methods in terms of both extracting text and identifying regional relationships.

The interaction between the spin-orbit coupling of thin film materials and two-dimensional ferromagnets is a critical area of study in the development of 2D magnetoelectronics. Experiments have shown varying results on spin-orbit torque in valley Hall devices made from InAs/EuS, which can be attributed to differences in how the materials are bonded at an atomic level. Our research reveals that the position of the conduction band in InAs relative to the valence band in EuS significantly impacts spin-orbit torque. Using density functional theory, we found that surface reconstructions and atomic repositioning can cause the materials' band structures to overlap or remain separate. When the bands overlap, spin-orbit torque is observed, whereas isolated bands result in no observable spin-orbit torque.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Furthermore, we have developed an optimized method to convert any given reduction to a specific class within the Borel Wadge hierarchy to $\Pi^0_1$-definite representatives of that hierarchy in a uniform and optimal manner.

Deep learning models, specifically convolutional neural networks, have been widely adopted for various computer vision tasks, including image classification and object detection. However, these applications require substantial labeled datasets, which can be costly and time-consuming to create. The data annotation process is further complicated by the need for precise bounding boxes, making it a time-consuming and error-prone process. To address these challenges, we introduce ClickTrain, a novel and efficient training framework that only necessitates user clicks for data annotation. By leveraging these clicks, we generate high-quality bounding boxes, which in turn lead to improved network performance compared to existing point-based frameworks like Detectron. In addition to its improved accuracy, ClickTrain also offers a significant speed advantage, outperforming comparable models like R-CNN and YOLOv3 by margins of up to 100 times, while maintaining comparable or better accuracy.

This research examines the properties of specific types of mathematical structures, referred to as subvarieties of non-commutative BL-algebras. We establish a correspondence between these subvarieties and certain subsets of a larger collection of structures, known as the Heyting subvariety generators, by analyzing their relationships in terms of inclusion and a specific binary operation. Furthermore, we establish mathematical formulas that define this binary operation based on set operations. Our findings are supported by a mathematical representation of the BL-algebraic structure through a combination of order and topology.

A new research project has been conducted, which involves the detection of planets using the X-shooter spectrograph on the Large Binocular Telescope. The study focuses on close stars within a specific gravity range, which are suitable for detecting planets. The team discovered 12 new planets and confirmed the existence of 109 other stars with planets. The newly found planets have masses ranging from 1 to 10 times the mass of Jupiter and are located at distances of up to 2.5 times the radius of the host star. The host stars in this project have a wide range of metallic content. The study's results show that giant planets tend to form around stars with higher metallic content, which is consistent with previous findings. The host stars in this project are generally older, which is consistent with the age of the planets. The study's findings suggest that the presence of giant planets is influenced by the metallic content of the host star, the age of the star, and the distance of the planet from the host star. Sequential decision-making problems under uncertainty can be effectively addressed using a probabilistic framework known as Markov decision processes. Operations research has utilized this framework to develop optimal solutions for various operations management issues, such as dynamic pricing and inventory management, often subject to constraints like a capped mark-up or liquidity levels. However, most existing methods for solving constrained Markov decision processes are too computationally intensive to be applied in real-time. This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm capable of finding an approximate, near-optimal policy quickly, even under constraint limitations. The proposed method leverages Lagrangian dual decomposition and employs the projected gradient descent algorithm to converge towards a satisfactory solution. The approach is further enhanced by incorporating a projection step that guarantees feasibility in relation to the constraint. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the proposed method's superior performance, outmaneuvering traditional alternatives and yielding significant improvements, including up to a 30% increase in expected profits and avoidance of constraint violations.

This research introduces a new dataset of handwritten mathematical symbols, 
which are also being analyzed using multiple NLP approaches to determine their 
formatting and semantic equivalence. The extensive dataset encompasses a total 
of 11,500 images, which are represented in various forms and arrangements, 
including 19,500 sentences generated by human writers. The proposed dataset, 
which is being used to validate the performance of multiple neural network models, 
will be made available for public access.

A proposed duality in superconformal quantum mechanics has been explored, suggesting a link between BPS states and twisted Dolbeault cohomology on a modified resolved space. This proposed duality, suggesting a holographic principle, can be seen as an altered version of the MKSS duality, which relates BPS states to twisted Betti cohomology classes in a related field theory context. Our findings show that Minkowski space's isometries translate to symmetries in the modified resolved space's complex structure. Additionally, we observed that certain Hodge numbers in this modified resolved space follow a pattern consistent with representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$.

This study examines how different network structures and the homogeneity of connections impact the spread of diseases that arise from interconnected individuals who exchange information. We investigate the SIS model of disease spread within a framework that incorporates network-based interactions. Our analysis reveals that the presence of self-loops and multi-edges in the network significantly contributes to higher disease prevalence and prolonged outbreaks compared to networks that lack these features. We demonstrate that the network's connectivity and degree distribution are key factors that determine disease prevalence and the duration of outbreaks. Moreover, we find that the centralization of connections in the network results in higher disease prevalence and longer outbreaks. We also explore the impact of removing self-loops and multi-edges from the network and discover that such removal significantly reduces disease prevalence and leads to shorter outbreaks. We propose a novel approach to minimize disease prevalence by selectively removing links in the network, and find that eliminating self-loops and multi-edges is an efficient strategy to achieve this goal. Our research provides valuable insights into the role of network structure in the spread of diseases and may inform the development of targeted public health interventions.

Reinforcement learning's high variance in policy gradient algorithms can be mitigated by using actor-critic methods, but these have limitations such as local optima and slow exploration. We propose an integration of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and actor-critic methods, enabled by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo's ability to globally traverse the policy space and, in certain cases, exactly compute sufficient gradient estimates. Building on previous methods like natural policy gradient, our new technique allows for exact exploration of discrete action spaces, and our experiments demonstrate improved efficiency and optimal policy convergence in complex tasks.

Any number $p \geq 5$ can be represented in the form $6k \pm 1$ for some integer $k$. In this paper, we examine equations of the form $6k \pm 1 = x^2 \pm y^3$, where $p = 6k \pm 1$. In particular, if $p$ is a prime number, we demonstrate that there cannot be integers $x$ and $y$ that satisfy this equation.

In diverse environments with challenging obstacles and adverse weather conditions like smoke, snow, and water, typical sensing technologies may not work effectively, making it difficult for robots to use standard methods for navigation and manipulation. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a new approach that utilizes the magnetic properties of materials to assist robots in navigating the environment. This approach involves magnetizing items in the scene and sensing the resulting magnetic field to create a map of the environment that can be used to facilitate sensing, navigation, and manipulation. To validate this concept, a series of experiments were conducted using a magnetized rod to represent a simulated object, and the results showed that combining magnetic sensing with other modalities can provide a more robust and effective way to navigate the environment.

A comprehensive spectral analysis of approximately 10000001-000000 objects from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) database has been conducted. This massive dataset has enabled the creation of precise classification algorithms for various celestial bodies, including comets, asteroids, and planets. By applying these sophisticated methods, a large collection of previously unclassified objects has been accurately categorized. This new collection has revealed significant patterns in the spectral characteristics of various celestial bodies, such as the diversity of chondrite types and the identification of new mineralogical components. These findings have also provided valuable insights into the spatial distribution and abundance of these celestial bodies in the solar system.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of size $n \times n$ over a finite field of size $q$, and consider the left $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$-module $M$ of column vectors of size $n$. The submodules of $M$ that are not freely cyclic are arranged geometrically as points in an affine plane of order $q$. The submodules that are freely cyclic form the lines of the same affine plane, excluding a standard projective plane line at infinity. The submodules of $M$ that are neither freely cyclic nor circular correspond to the points of the standard projective plane of order $q$, located infinitely so.

In a 1984 publication in Israel Journal of Mathematics, three specific models were analyzed: the first involved adding $\mathfrak{c}^{+}$ Cohen reals over $L$, the second involved adding $\mathfrak{c}^{+}$ random reals over $L$, and the third involved adding $\mathfrak{c}^{+}$ random reals over a Cohen extension with $\mathfrak{c}$ many reals. These models were shown to each have the property that their respective continuum was not covered by any of their respective extensions. This paper aims to demonstrate that the properties of the models analyzed in the above publication can be fully captured by extending a base model with the ultimate Cohen or random forcing, under the condition that the base model's continuum is equivalent to its cardinality of the reals.

A new approach to learning optimal dynamic treatment regimes online is proposed, incorporating observational data into the framework of Bayesian reinforcement learning. By utilizing a Bayesian generalized linear model, the method enables the calculation of average treatment effects and shrinks towards an external prior that accounts for confounding variables. The pessimism principle's integration with the Bayesian LTLR model facilitates accurate model assessments, while the proposed shrinkage method's efficacy is demonstrated through rigorous statistical analysis. The online algorithm's convergence is confirmed, and the approach's performance is validated through experiments on artificial data and the NCI-60 cell line study, as well as a cell apoptosis case study.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be established through bicomplexe functors, as demonstrated by a recent finding regarding the functors between complete exact categories defined by Auslander and Whitehead. Building on this result, we present a streamlined proof of Miyashita's duality theorem, which shows that the functors DHom_T(-): Ho(Stil_T) -> Ho(Stil_S) and DHom_S(-): Ho(Stil_S) -> Ho(End_T) are equivalent to certain derived functors, given that T and S are tilting modules over rings A and B, respectively, with End_A(T) being Morita equivalent to B.

A proposed model for $E_8$ symmetry involves a discrete torus with its coordinates defined by the root system of $E_8$, coordinate values restricted to octonions, and its magnitude governed by the Minkowski metric, all packaged into the form of $|Y^{\mu}e_{\mu}>(\text{mod } 2)$. The aim is to demonstrate the emergence of the Lie algebra $E_8$ from the proposed model.

Theoretical models suggest a unique type of superconducting state exists in flat band systems, where Cooper pairs condense but unpaired electrons are unable to move. We investigate the low-energy excitations of this flat band superconductor using neutron scattering, which probes both charge and spin dynamics. Our research demonstrates that, despite the non-mobile unpaired electrons, these system's excitations resemble those of a conventional superconductor, with a key difference: it supports in-phase and out-of-phase modes for charge and spin dynamics, which can be experimentally distinguished.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a priori conditions that hold for the distribution of the involved random variables.

Presence-absence data is a crucial component of ecological studies, encompassing data such as species distribution, biodiversity assessments, and community analysis. Due to the inherent challenges of collecting such data, which often results in 0/1 values representing absence or presence, statistical analysis of presence-absence data poses difficulties. A common approach to address this issue involves the application of the logit transformation, which enables researchers to utilize standard linear modeling methods. However, the reliability of this method heavily depends on the accuracy of absence data, which is often challenging to obtain. A novel paper introduces an alternative transformation method that takes into account uncertainty in absence data, specifically drawing from the sensitivity analysis of ecological monitoring systems. The SAA transformation conceptually represents an average state between absence and presence, offering a more realistic interpretation of absence data. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the SAA transformation through case studies involving vegetation and bird biodiversity assessments.

This research introduces a novel, fully convolutional network architecture for salient object detection based on a densely connected design. The network incorporates a cross-attention based feature extraction method to produce separate salency maps for vertical and horizontal dimensions, which are then combined to form a comprehensive salency representation. A densely connected structure is utilized to iteratively refine these representations for enhanced accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed approach necessitates no data augmentation and employs a multi-task learning strategy to simultaneously predict multiple types of salency maps.

The fourth edition of the 2019 SemEval sub-competition focused on identifying and categorizing hate speech, a task that required participants to classify 10 distinct categories of content. To accomplish this, we utilized a pre-trained word vector model called FastText, which was then optimized through fine-tuning on the provided dataset. For categorizing the content, we employed a neural network-based classifier called Keras. The experiment revealed that our approach achieved high levels of accuracy and F1 scores, with the results further enhanced by incorporating additional features such as tweet length and character n-grams.

A number is considered palindromic if its numerical representation mirrors itself. Specifically, this work focuses on numbers that are not just palindromic in base 10, but also when represented in base 2. The findings from an extensive search for such numbers, up to 10 billion, are presented along with related statistical observations. The associated probability related to these discoveries is discussed.

Computed tomography (CT) is an established imaging technique, but its traditional assumption of monoenergetic X-rays does not hold in modern polyenergetic X-ray sources. This discrepancy can result in various artifacts such as beam hardening, scatter, and noise correlations, thereby compromising the accuracy of CT image-derived data. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the Bayesian scatter and distortion correction (BSCDC) algorithm, which aims to mitigate these effects through a combination of statistical modeling and optimization. This study presents an enhanced version of BSCDC, which incorporates a data-driven approach to reduce computational complexity and increase robustness. The improved method achieves a notable reduction in computational time while maintaining comparable performance to the original BSCDC, as demonstrated through simulations and experiments using a cone-beam CT scanner.

Handwritten text recognition in low resource settings presents significant challenges, mainly due to the scarcity of available data. One key factor contributing to this issue is the limited number of historical documents that have been preserved. This problem is compounded by the difficulty of creating and labeling datasets, which requires considerable time and expertise. To address these limitations, researchers have developed an innovative framework for enhancing handwritten text recognition in resource-constrained environments. The framework leverages the benefits of few-shot learning and loopless generative adversarial networks to create a data augmentation strategy that effectively increases the size of training datasets. By incorporating this data augmentation technique into modern handwritten text recognition models, the framework demonstrates impressive performance on diverse datasets, including varied scripts and non-standard writing styles.

strength functions for the $^{48}$Ca and $^{66}$Ni nuclei, utilizing the
Symanzik-inspired, improved Hermitian (SYI) version of the
independent-particle random-phase approximation (IPRPY). This involves
constructing the Hamiltonian matrix from the Hamiltonian matrix elements,
using the Monte-Carlo shell-model (MCSM) Hamiltonian for each nucleus,
calculations were limited by the maximum number of $f$-shell orbitals included
and the maximum number of excitations considered. This approach has
previously been successful in determining binding energies and energy levels
of several nuclei, but to our knowledge, it is the first time this method has
been applied to compute $B(\E1)$ and $B(\E2)$ strength functions.
Our results for these strength functions have been compared to experimental data
and to results from the large-scale shell-model (LSD) method, with the
computation limited by the maximum number of excitations considered.

been found to be in good agreement with the experimental data, with the
